name: Can You Feel It
description: “Can You Feel It” is a 1986 Chicago house track by Mr. Fingers — the recording alias of Chicago producer Larry Heard — and one of the foundational records of deep house. Heard, a former drummer, built the track with a Roland synthesizer and a TR-909 drum machine, layering parts between two cassette decks in single passes. Trax Records released it as an instrumental on the Washing Machine EP in 1986, and it later appeared on the 1988 Fingers Inc. album Another Side. An unauthorized later version layered Chuck Roberts' spoken “My House” sermon over the instrumental; it became the version many dancers know best, and Heard has publicly disavowed it. The record's impact on deep house is routinely compared to the impact of Derrick May's “Strings of Life” on Detroit techno.

name: Civil Rights Act of 1964
description: The Civil Rights Act of 1964, signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson on July 2, 1964, is the foundational statute of modern American civil rights law. Passed after the longest filibuster in Senate history to that date — broken by cloture on June 10, 1964, the first time the Senate had ever voted to end debate on a civil rights bill — the Act outlawed segregation and discrimination in public accommodations (Title II), barred discrimination in federally assisted programs (Title VI), and prohibited employment discrimination by race, color, religion, sex, or national origin (Title VII), creating the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to enforce it. It answered, in law, the demands carried through Montgomery, Birmingham, the March on Washington, and the Mississippi summer then underway; President Kennedy had called for it in June 1963, eight days after George Wallace stood in the schoolhouse door, and Johnson drove it through a grieving Congress as Kennedy's memorial. name: Carl Davis

description: Carl H. Davis (September 19, 1934 – August 9, 2012) was a Chicago record producer and executive, one of the principal architects of the Chicago soul sound. From 1962 he was a producer and A&R director at Columbia's OKeh subsidiary, producing hits for Major Lance and others, often with Curtis Mayfield songs. In the mid-1960s he took creative charge of Brunswick Records' Chicago operation, producing Jackie Wilson's comeback hits including the million-seller '(Your Love Keeps Lifting Me) Higher and Higher,' Barbara Acklin's 'Love Makes a Woman,' and the Chi-Lites, who had signed to Brunswick after meeting Davis in 1968 and whose Brunswick years produced 'Have You Seen Her' and 'Oh Girl.' He founded the Dakar label in 1967, with hits by Tyrone Davis (no relation), and later Chi-Sound Records. He died of pulmonary fibrosis at 77 in Summerville, South Carolina.

name: Charles White

description: Charles White, born Charles Wilbert White Jr. on April 2, 1918, on Chicago's South Side, was an American artist and a central figure of the Chicago Black Renaissance. The son of Ethelene Gary, a domestic servant, and Charles White Sr., a railroad and construction worker, he won a scholarship to the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in 1937 and painted the Federal Art Project mural Five Great American Negroes for the George Cleveland branch of the Chicago Public Library in 1939. His best-known work, The Contribution of the Negro to American Democracy, is the mural at Hampton University. White married the artist Elizabeth Catlett in 1941 (divorced 1946), worked in Mexico in 1946–47 in the circle of Siqueiros and Rivera at the Taller de Gráfica Popular, and settled in Los Angeles in 1956, teaching at the Otis Art Institute and winning election to the National Academy of Design in 1972. He died on October 3, 1979, in Los Angeles; his work is held by the Art Institute of Chicago, LACMA, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney, and the National Gallery of Art, and received its first major retrospective in 2018.

description: The Chitlin' Circuit was the informal network of theaters, nightclubs, ballrooms, and juke joints across the eastern, southern, and midwestern United States where Black musicians, comedians, and dancers worked during segregation, from the 1930s through the 1960s. It took shape after the 1930 collapse of the Theatre Owners Booking Association, when Black Indianapolis entrepreneurs Sea and Denver D. Venues ranged from rural juke joints to first-class theaters; singer Ruth Brown held that an artist had made it by playing four of them: the Regal in Chicago, the Howard in Washington, the Uptown in Philadelphia, and the Apollo in New York. In Chicago its documented stops included the Regal Theater, Club DeLisa, and Robert's Show Lounge. The circuit trained generations of Black performers and helped carry blues and R&B toward rock 'n' roll.

name: Colson Whitehead
description: Arch Colson Chipp Whitehead, known as Colson Whitehead, is an American novelist born on November 6, 1969, in New York City and raised in Manhattan. He graduated from Harvard University in 1991 with a degree in English and comparative literature and then wrote criticism for The Village Voice. His first novel, The Intuitionist (1999), follows a Black elevator inspector investigating a conspiracy. John Henry Days (2001) reworks the John Henry folk legend, and his later novels include Apex Hides the Hurt (2006), Sag Harbor (2009), and the post-apocalyptic Zone One (2011); The Colossus of New York (2003) collected his essays on the city. The Underground Railroad (2016), which reimagines the escape network as an actual underground railway, won the National Book Award for Fiction and the 2017 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. The Nickel Boys (2019), set at a Jim Crow-era Florida reform school, won the 2020 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, making him the fourth writer to win two Pulitzer Prizes in the fiction category; it also won the Kirkus Prize and the Orwell Prize for Political Fiction. Harlem Shuffle, a crime novel opening in 1959, followed in 2021. His honors include a MacArthur Fellowship in 2002 and the Library of Congress Prize for American Fiction in 2020.

name: Countee Cullen
description: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) was among the most celebrated poets of the Harlem Renaissance. Born Countee LeRoy Porter — likely in Louisville, Kentucky, though some accounts say New York — he was orphaned young and, at fifteen, taken into the Harlem home of the Reverend Frederick A. Cullen, pastor of Salem Methodist Episcopal Church, whose name he took. At DeWitt Clinton High School and then New York University he won prize after prize for poetry, and in 1925 — the year he graduated from NYU and entered Harvard's master's program — he published Color, the first book of a major Renaissance career. Writing in the Romantic tradition of Keats and Shelley, Cullen insisted a poet be judged as a poet rather than a “Negro poet,” yet race charged his finest work, from “Heritage” to “Incident” to “Yet Do I Marvel.” He edited the landmark anthology Caroling Dusk (1927), published Copper Sun (1927) and The Black Christ (1929), won a Guggenheim fellowship, and in 1928 married W. E. B. Du Bois's daughter Yolande in one of Harlem's great social events. From 1934 he taught in New York public schools, mentoring a young James Baldwin, and he died in 1946 at forty-two.

name: Chicago Black Renaissance
description: The Chicago Black Renaissance was the creative movement that flowered in Chicago's South Side Black Belt — Bronzeville — from the 1930s through the 1950s, when writers, visual artists, dancers, scholars, and musicians built a self-consciously Black urban culture out of the Great Migration's raw material. Its literary core — Richard Wright, Margaret Walker, Gwendolyn Brooks, Willard Motley, and the South Side Writers Group — turned away from the Harlem Renaissance's folk retrospect toward a literary naturalism of kitchenettes, stockyards, and South Side streets, theorized in Wright's "Blueprint for Negro Writing" and crowned when Brooks's Annie Allen won the Pulitzer Prize in 1950. Its institutions were community-built: Vivian G. Harsh's Hall Branch Library, whose Special Negro Collection and Book Review and Lecture Forum made a public library the movement's salon; the South Side Community Art Center, opened in 1940 and dedicated by Eleanor Roosevelt in 1941; the Illinois Writers' Project; and the Chicago Defender's pages. In visual art, Archibald Motley, Charles White, Eldzier Cortor, and Margaret Burroughs painted and organized; in music, Thomas A. Dorsey's gospel and the South Side's blues and jazz carried the same neighborhoods into sound. More working-class, more politically radical, and far less dependent on white patrons than Harlem's Renaissance, Chicago's movement was documented as it happened by St. Clair Drake and Horace Cayton's Black Metropolis — and it seeded the Black-run institutions, above all Burroughs's DuSable Museum, that carried Black Chicago culture into the civil-rights era.

Built at the turn of the twentieth century — its construction date is disputed in the sources, as the record notes — and recorded in City of Chicago landmark survey data under the name Inter-State Building, the structure first served as a synagogue for Congregation B'nai Sholom; the Chicago Historic Resources Survey lists the Defender Publishing Company as owner by 1921. From 1920 to 1960 the building housed the Defender's newsroom and publishing operations. On September 9, 1998, it was designated a Chicago Landmark as one of the nine structures of the Black Metropolis–Bronzeville District. It stands today as a landmark of Black media infrastructure — the physical plant of a paper that functioned as an institution.

description: The Pentecostal denomination rooted in the Holiness movement whose Chicago congregations formed a significant share of the storefront landscape. Founded 1907 by Bishop Charles Harrison Mason; headquartered at Mason Temple, Memphis.

name: Chicago Sister Cities International
description: City of Chicago's official sister-cities program; formal municipal link to Accra, Durban and Casablanca. City program coordinating Chicago's sister-city relationships; a division of World Business Chicago.

name: Chuck Berry
description: Rock-and-roll guitarist and songwriter (1926–2017); recorded "Maybellene" for Chess Records in May 1955 after Muddy Waters referred him to Leonard Chess; inaugural Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductee (1986).

name: Cheikh Anta Diop
description: Senegalese historian, anthropologist and physicist; Director of the Radiocarbon Laboratory at IFAN, University of Dakar; argued the African origin of pharaonic Egyptian civilization ('The African Origin of Civilization', 1974); lectured to Chicago's CCICS study-tour group at the University of Dakar in 1977.

name: Chicago Free South Africa Movement
description: Chicago anti-apartheid organizing formation active from 1984. Helped organize demonstrations from November 1984 to March 1985 in front of the South African Consulate on South Michigan Street to urge city divestment from apartheid South Africa. Organizer Alice Palmer was arrested in a January 1985 protest; she and eight fellow protesters were tried and acquitted under the Law of Necessity. Members were instrumental in bringing Nelson Mandela to Chicago for his July 1993 visit, a two-and-a-half-day trip with six fundraising events during which Mandela received the key to the city from Mayor Richard M. Daley.

name: Center for Inner City Studies (NEIU)
aliases: Jacob H. Carruthers Center for Inner City Studies; CCICS
description: Northeastern Illinois University’s Jacob H. Carruthers Center for Inner City Studies at 700 E. Oakwood Blvd., Chicago; African-centered urban research and degree programs; organized the 1977 Nile Valley study tour and housed the Kemetic Institute.

name: Chicago City Council
description: The legislative branch of the government of the city of Chicago, Illinois: 50 alderpersons elected from 50 wards to four-year terms, meeting in the Council Chambers in Chicago City Hall with the mayor as presiding officer. Established as the Common Council in 1837, renamed City Council in 1876; the modern 50-ward form dates to 1923. Passed a December 3, 1984 resolution condemning apartheid (introduced by 29th Ward Alderman Danny K. Davis) and a July 12, 1990 anti-apartheid ordinance with banking and selective-purchasing provisions (effective October 31, 1990). Approved the Bronzeville Lakefront redevelopment on July 31, 2021.

name: Casablanca, Morocco
description: Moroccan city; Chicago's oldest African sister city (1982), with documented government, cultural and youth exchanges.

name: Clifton Dillon
description: Jamaican reggae/dancehall producer; relocated to Chicago and established the Solid Gold sound system (Chicago International Reggae Award, Best Discotheque); produced Shabba Ranks, Patra, and Mad Cobra.

name: Chuck Wren
description: Chicago ska DJ; host of "Everything Off-Beat" since 1989; founder of Jump Up Records (1993); runs Chicago's longest-running ska/reggae night at Delilah's.

name: Carla Acevedo-Yates
description: Puerto Rican curator; the Marilyn and Larry Fields Curator at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. Curated 'Dancing the Revolution: From Dancehall to Reggaetón' (2026), 'Forecast Form: Art in the Caribbean Diaspora 1990s–Today' (2022), and 'entre horizontes: Art and Activism Between Chicago and Puerto Rico' (2023–2024); leads the MCA's Hemispheric Initiative.

name: Consulate of Jamaica in Chicago
description: Jamaica's Honorary Consulate in Chicago at 4655 S. Martin Luther King Drive #201 (Grand Boulevard), headed by Honorary Consul Lester Barclay; supervised by the Embassy of Jamaica in Washington, D.C.

name: Consulate General of Haiti in Chicago
description: Consulate General of Haiti in Chicago at 11 East Adams Street, Suite 1400 (Chicago Loop), headed by Consul General Lesly Conde; in 2026 it estimated that around 40,000 self-reported Haitians had settled in Chicago.

name: Chicago Concerned Jamaicans
description: Chicago-based Jamaican diaspora organization established in 1988 by Jimmy and Daphne Lopez with other members of the Jamaican community, originally to raise Hurricane Gilbert relief. After the relief effort, the board shifted the organization's focus solely to educating Jamaican youth. About 50 members strong; provides roughly 35 high school scholarships annually (44 across all 14 parishes in 2013) and has contributed just over US$700,000 to Jamaican education over its first 25 years through books, computers, scholarships, and library improvements. Its annual fall dinner-dance fundraiser provides most of the scholarship money.

name: CaribNation
description: Northwestern University's Caribbean student association (founded circa 1998), uplifting Caribbean students through countries of the month, carnival bands, the annual CaribFest celebration, and the annual J'ouvert on the Lakefill.

name: Caribbean Festival (CAF)
description: Ephraim Malachi Martin launched the Caribbean Festival (CAF) in Chicago in 2004, staged in the north and west loop areas.

name: CaribFest (Northwestern University)
description: Northwestern University's CaribNation held the third annual CaribFest in May 2002 and the fourth annual CaribFest in May 2003, celebrating Caribbean culture with speakers and music; the 2002 event featured Chicago-based reggae band Indika, and the 2003 event featured Evanston-based Haitian band Sakad and Jamaican singer Devon Brown.

name: Chano Pozo
description: Cuban conguero (1915–1948); first Latin percussionist in Dizzy Gillespie's band; co-wrote 'Manteca' and 'Tin Tin Deo'; a founder of Latin jazz. His autumn-1948 Chicago performance with Gillespie's big band at the Pershing Ballroom is an early verified Cuban-musician Chicago appearance.

name: Celia Cruz
aliases: Úrsula Hilaria Celia Caridad Cruz Alfonso
description: Cuban singer known as the Queen of Salsa and 'La Guarachera de Cuba'; lead singer of La Sonora Matancera (1950–1965); trademark shout '¡Azúcar!'; documented Chicago performances include the Aragon Ballroom in spring 1995 and Fiesta Boricua-era appearances.

name: Chucho Valdés
aliases: Dionisio Jesús Valdés Rodríguez; Jesús Valdés
description: Cuban pianist, bandleader, composer and arranger; son of Bebo Valdés; founded the landmark Afro-Cuban jazz band Irakere in 1973; multiple Grammy and Latin Grammy winner. His Afro-Cuban suite La Creación was co-commissioned by Chicago's Symphony Center and premiered in 2021.

name: Carlos Hernández Falcón
description: Chicago-born Puerto Rican arts leader and cultural advocate; founded the Puerto Rican Arts Alliance in his home's basement in 1996 and served as its executive director for nearly 28 years; honored by the Illinois House and the Chicago City Council.

name: Chicago Philharmonic
description: Chicago orchestra that partnered with the Puerto Rican Arts Alliance on a 2021 Puerto Rican music collaboration; musician-governed orchestra founded from the Lyric Opera Orchestra principals.

name: Chicago Latino Theater Alliance (CLATA)
description: Alliance founded in 2016 by executive director Myrna Salazar with Chicago's three most prominent Latino arts organizations: the National Museum of Mexican Art, the International Latino Cultural Center, and the Puerto Rican Arts Alliance. A nonprofit 501(c)(3), it produces Destinos, the Chicago International Latino Theater Festival, aiming to build the country's leading international Latino theater festival while giving local companies organizational, marketing, and financial support and working toward a permanent home for Chicago's Latino theater artists. The 3rd Destinos (2019) presented 93+ performances; the 5th ran September 14-October 16, 2022, dedicated to Salazar after her death in August 2022.

name: Chuck Nessa
description: Chicago jazz producer; managed Bob Koester's Jazz Record Mart and supervised Roscoe Mitchell's 1966 Delmark "Sound" sessions; founded Nessa Records (1967), documenting the early AACM sessions.

name: Celeste Alexander (DJ Celeste)
description: Hyde Park native; one of Chicago's first female house DJs. Began DJing in 1982 after being told hot-mixing 'wasn't really for women'; lead DJ of the all-female Fantastic Four crew; the only woman to play the Music Box alongside Ron Hardy; Chicago DJ Hall of Fame inductee.

name: Chicago steppers community
description: Chicago-style steppin' took shape on the South and West sides in the 1940s-1950s, evolving from the 'Bop' (a term used until the early 1970s, itself derived from east coast swing dances); college station WKKC 89.3 programmed steppers music as early as 1975, and WVAZ 102.7 FM gave it commercial radio footing in 1989.

name: Chicago footwork/juke community
description: Footwork dance and music emerged in the 1990s-2000s from house parties, ghettos, and underground dance competitions on Chicago's South and West sides, with dancers and producers pushing each other; the scene persisted through Dance Mania's 2001 closure and broke internationally via YouTube dance videos.

name: Chosen Few DJs
description: The Chosen Few DJs, founded by Wayne Williams in 1977 with Jesse Saunders, Tony Hatchett, Alan King, Andre Hatchett (later joined by Terry Hunter and Mike Dunn), played soulful dance music at historic South Side spots including Sauer's, First Impressions, the Playground, and the Loft.

name: Chess Records pressing plant
description: Chess Records’ pressing operations: Midwest Record Pressing, Inc. at 4750 S. Cottage Grove Ave. (late 1950s-1960s, run by James Gann) and the Ter-Mar pressing plant at the 320 E. 21st St. headquarters (1968-1969).

name: Chicago stepping community
description: Stepping is sustained through South and West Side social events called "sets," competitions including the World's Largest Steppers Competition, and intergenerational transmission. The partner dance evolved from the Chicago Bop of the late 1950s–1960s; Sam Chatman ("Godfather of Steppin'") coined the name "Stepping" in 1974.

name: Chicago footwork battle community
aliases: Chicago footwork community; footwork battle community
description: Chicago footwork is a late-1990s/early-2000s dance and music ecology derived from ghetto house and juke, with DJ–dancer feedback at its center. Key figures include RP Boo, DJ Rashad, DJ Spinn, and DJ Clent: RP Boo's "Baby Come On" (1997) is considered the founding track, and DJ Clent's 1998 Beatdown House circle (Spinn, Rashad, Boo, and others) originated the sound.

name: Curtis — Curtis Mayfield
description: Curtis (1970) was Curtis Mayfield's debut solo album on Curtom, launching his independent career after the Impressions with socially conscious soul including '(Don't Worry) If There's a Hell Below, We're All Going to Go.'.

name: Chicago Jazz Archive (University of Chicago)
description: The Chicago Jazz Archive at the University of Chicago collects and preserves materials on Chicago jazz history, with a research guide pointing to related collections including the Walter Henri Dyett Papers. The archive's cross-reference to the Dyett Papers demonstrates the archival network linking university, public-library, and school-based Black music collections.

name: Chicago History Museum music holdings
description: The Chicago History Museum holds music-related collections documenting the city's performance history, including materials on Black venues, theaters, and musicians. The museum tier complements archives and libraries by holding artifacts, posters, and ephemera — the material culture of the music scene.

name: Chess Records masters / catalog archive (commercial)
description: The Chess Records master recordings and catalog constitute a commercial archive of the Chicago blues and R&B canon, now held through successive corporate owners. Reissue programs from the Chess masters are the primary channel through which the 1950s–60s Chicago studio sound reaches contemporary listeners.

name: Carter Broadcast Group (KPRS/KPRT)
description: Kansas City family-owned Black radio group founded in 1950 by Andrew 'Skip' Carter; KPRS is the oldest continuously African American-owned and operated radio station in the US (FCC), home of KPRS-FM 'Hot 103 Jamz' and KPRT gospel.

name: Cathy Hughes
description: Founder of Radio One/Urban One (1980); the central individual figure in Black radio’s survival through consolidation and the creator of the ‘Quiet Storm’ format; first African American woman to head a publicly traded corporation (1999 IPO).

name: Charlamagne Tha God
aliases: Lenard Larry McKelvey; Lenard McKelvey; Charlamagne
description: Radio host and media entrepreneur (Lenard Larry McKelvey, b. 1978); co-host of The Breakfast Club since 2010; founder of the Black Effect Podcast Network (iHeartMedia JV) and the Mental Wealth Alliance.

name: Comcast NBCUniversal diversity commitment
description: The FCC diversity commitments attached to the January 18, 2011 Comcast-NBCUniversal merger approval: increased carriage of diverse networks, 10 new independent channels by 2019, Internet Essentials low-income broadband. The regulatory engine behind the 2012-2013 wave of Black cable networks (ASPiRE, BabyFirst Americas, REVOLT, El Rey).

name: Copyright Uncertainty
description: Orphan works, expired licenses, and adverse precedent chilling digitization, publication, and classroom use of Black historical materials. Adverse precedent includes the Second Circuit’s 2024 affirmance against the Internet Archive’s controlled digital lending (Hachette v. Internet Archive).

name: Collector Death
description: Death of the private collector/custodian with no succession plan: the mortality-driven window in which estates are dispersed, discarded, or sold before any institution intervenes.

name: Chicago Defender Photo Morgue
description: The photographic morgue of the Chicago Defender (1905-): ~250,000 images counted by volunteer Angela Ford; the visual record of the Great Migration era.

name: Chess Records Masters (destroyed)
description: The master recordings of Chess Records (Chuck Berry, Muddy Waters, Howlin’ Wolf, et al.), destroyed in the June 1, 2008 Universal Studios vault fire (Building 6197); exact Chess title-by-title losses contested.

name: Chicago Whip Morgue
description: The morgue and business records of the Chicago Whip (1919-1939; 65,000 circulation within a year; "Don't Spend Money Where You Can't Work" campaign): no publicly documented archive located.

name: Calhoun-McCormick Photographic Archive
description: The roughly 30-year film archive of New Orleans photographers Keith Calhoun and Chandra McCormick documenting Black New Orleanian life — secured in bins before the 2005 Hurricane Katrina evacuation; two-thirds destroyed by floodwater; the salvaged negatives were frozen, scanned, and reprinted as new work.

name: Chicago Public Library
description: TYPE CORRECTION (RELP8, 2026-10-06): previously mistyped as Person. The municipal public library system of the City of Chicago, founded 1872/opened 1873; operates the Harold Washington Library Center and branches across the city's 77 community areas; custodian of the Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection (Carter G. Woodson Regional Library).

name: Carnegie Museum of Art
description: Pittsburgh art museum founded in 1895 by Andrew Carnegie; custodian since 2001 of Charles 'Teenie' Harris's roughly 80,000 negatives documenting Black Pittsburgh life; runs a public-identification program for the Harris archive.

name: Center for Southeast Louisiana Studies
description: Research center at Southeastern Louisiana University (Hammond, LA) preserving the history and cultures of Louisiana’s Florida Parishes and surrounding areas; maintains the SLU Archives and Special Collections (~600 collections); custodian of the Richard Funeral Home records of Lake Charles.

name: CBMR defunding threat
aliases: 2012 Center for Black Music Research prioritization threat; Columbia College CBMR budget-cut threat
description: (2012) Columbia College's 2012 prioritization process proposing to eliminate the Center for Black Music Research's funding after ~70% budget cuts since 2006.

name: Carter G. Woodson
description: Founder of the ASNLH (1915) at the Wabash YMCA; originator of Negro History Week (1926), the direct origin of Black History Month.

name: Cora Carroll
description: Black businesswoman; held the promotional Chicago Defender title Mayor of Bronzeville in the 1960s. Photographed riding in the Bud Billiken Day parade (1966–1968). Identity check 2026-10-06: no birth/death dates published in cited sources.

name: Chicago Lawn (community area 66)
description: Chicago Lawn's African-American share: 0.0% (1970), 10.2% (1980), 26.2% (1990), 52.5% (2000), 49.3% (2010), 50.8% (2013) — a later transition than the eastern 63rd corridor.

name: Crown Propeller Lounge
description: Premier 63rd Street R&B and jazz lounge of the 1950s, owned by Norman Schlossberg; hosted Miles Davis, Illinois Jacquet, The Flamingos, and others. A Hammond organ was a house feature (Chicago Daily Defender, Oct 1956); the club's illuminated sign appeared in the opening of the 1980s TV series Crime Stories.

name: Club Bagdad
description: South Side jazz club at 840 E. 63rd Street, documented in the Chicago Defender's October 10, 1953 nightlife listings (the 5 Blazes and Terry Timmons).

name: Cotton Club
description: 1950s Woodlawn jazz club at 6249 S. Cottage Grove Avenue, documented in the October 10, 1953 Chicago Defender (Harold King and Red Allen). A namesake of the Harlem Cotton Club; distinct from both the New York original and the later 1986-2006 South Loop club.

name: C and C Lounge
description: South Side jazz lounge at 6513 S. Cottage Grove, Chicago — just south of East 63rd Street in Woodlawn's 63rd–Cottage Grove nightlife district. Chicago Defender listings (Nov. 22, 1961) billed Tom Archer and Porter Kilbert, Dave McCullough, Bill Hobbs, and Lowell Pointer at the room.

name: Carr's Discount Department Store
description: Discount department store at 610 W. 63rd Street in Chicago's Englewood neighborhood; opened October 30, 1958 in the former Southtown Theatre (closed August 1958); the building later became a flea market and was demolished in 1991.

name: College Inn
description: Major park restaurant on 63rd

name: Cottage Grove Rexall
description: Black Chicago commercial-strip drugstore documented via an archival photograph (Chicago Patterns, "63rd Street: heydays, remnants & risk"): a Rexall franchise storefront on the 63rd Street corridor near Cottage Grove Avenue in Woodlawn. The photograph is the sole documentary source; no incorporation/closure dates located.

name: CTA stations on/near 63rd (group)
aliases: 63rd Street CTA stations; Jackson Park / Englewood branch stations
description: Dorchester (1400 E. 63rd, closed 1/13/1973); University (1200 E. 63rd, closed 1994, demolished 1997); Cottage Grove (became East 63rd terminus 1996); Harvard (303 W. 63rd, closed 2/9/1992); Racine (6314-16 S. Racine, closed 1994, not reopened); Ashland/63rd (opened 5/6/1969, replaced Loomis terminal); 63rd Red Line (opened 9/26-28/1969, Dan Ryan median).

name: Chicago City Bank and Trust Co. Building (later Park National Bank)
aliases: Park National Bank Building (Englewood); Chicago City Bank and Trust Company Building
description: Former Chicago City Bank and Trust Co. Building (later Park National Bank), 815 W 63rd St, Englewood. Four-story Art Deco limestone bank building by Abraham Epstein; cornerstone reads "A.D. 1929"; the institution moved in February 24, 1930. Designated a Chicago local landmark October 8, 2008.

name: Cottage Grove CTA station (Green Line)
description: Opened April 23, 1893 (South Side Rapid Transit, built for World’s Columbian Exposition). Original station demolished 1989; replacement opened 1991; became East 63rd branch terminal May 12, 1996; track east of Cottage Grove removed. CTA lists it as an active Green Line station at 800 E. 63rd St, Woodlawn.

name: Chicago & Western Indiana 'Little' Englewood station
aliases: Englewood station (Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad); Little Englewood
description: Englewood passenger station of the Chicago & Western Indiana Railroad at 551 W 63rd St, Chicago — "Little" Englewood, distinct from the larger Englewood Union Station. Passenger service ended in two stages: December 13, 1965 (Erie-Lackawanna) and July 29, 1979 (Norfolk & Western); abandoned platforms and canopies were still visible from the CTA Green Line in 2013.

name: Chi Tech Collective
description: Chicago South Side community tech organization working on digital inclusion and tech workforce pathways; partnered with the Internet Equity Initiative and Blacks In Technology for a 2024 South Side Tech and Community Expo.

name: Chicago Conservator
description: Chicago's first Black newspaper, founded in 1878 by attorney Ferdinand Lee Barnett. Ida B. Wells wrote for it from 1893 and edited it from 1895 to 1897; it folded in 1914.

name: Chicago World (Chicago Enterprise)
aliases: Chicago World; The Chicago World; Chicago Enterprise
description: Black weekly founded by Jacob R. Tipper as the Chicago Enterprise and later renamed the Chicago World. Joel Augustus Rogers reported for it in the 1920s; Fay M. Jackson later edited it.

name: Clear View Group
description: Austin private equity firm; bought Ebony and Jet from JPC

name: Chandler Owen
description: Writer and editor; co-founded the radical journal The Messenger with A. Philip Randolph in 1917. Moved to Chicago, where he became managing editor of the Chicago Bee, founded his own public-relations company, and wrote speeches for presidential candidates and presidents.

name: Chester Commodore
description: African-American editorial cartoonist and comic-strip artist; Chicago Defender staff cartoonist 1948–2004. Created 'The Sparks' (1948), took over 'Bungleton Green' from Jay Jackson, and drew weekly full-page caricatures for the Defender's Accent arts supplement from 1974.

name: Chicago History Museum
description: The Chicago History Museum (1601 N. Clark St.) is a research repository whose collections CTL draws on across the graph; the graph record itself was created because the museum holds the Claude A. Barnett Papers. Its Abakanowicz Research Center holds printed and published materials, archives and manuscripts, prints and photographs, architectural drawings, and ephemera, and CTL's preservation brief records the center as free with no appointment required. The Barnett Papers run to four linear feet, including Defender-versus-Barnett correspondence, 1919 Associated Negro Press clippings, and 1949–64 Africa files, with a finding aid online. The museum also provides digital newspaper databases covering the Chicago Defender, Chicago Bee, Whip, and Broad Ax, and its own institutional histories anchor CTL claims elsewhere in the graph — its account of the Bud Billiken Parade's 1923 founding by Robert S. Abbott and Lucius Harper is graded VERIFIED in the Defender dossier. The record's alias preserves its former name, the Chicago Historical Society.

name: Chronicling America (LOC)
description: Open digitized runs of Broad Ax, Whip, World

name: Charlotte L. Lyons
description: Ebony magazine food editor (1984-2010) and operator of the Johnson Publishing test kitchen; wrote the monthly “A Date with a Dish” column; advisor to the Museum of Food and Drink’s “African/American: Making the Nation’s Table” exhibition.

name: Carl A. Hansberry
description: Prominent Black Chicago real-estate broker and banker whose 1937 purchase of a covenanted home led to the U.S. Supreme Court case Hansberry v. Lee (1940); father of playwright Lorraine Hansberry.

name: Chicago Housing Authority
description: Municipal corporation created in 1937 to own and operate public housing in Chicago; by 1960 the city's largest landlord. First director Elizabeth Wood (1937–1954); later infamous for segregated high-rise projects, the Gautreaux desegregation lawsuit, a 20-plus-year receivership, and the controversial Plan for Transformation.

name: Contract Buyers League
description: Grassroots organization founded in 1968 by North Lawndale residents — Clyde Ross (co-chairman), Ruth Wells, and organizer Jack Macnamara — to fight the predatory contract-selling system that stripped wealth from Black homebuyers. 500+ residents organized; picketing and a payment strike; two lawsuits failed.

name: Clyde Ross
description: North Lawndale homeowner and co-chairman of the Contract Buyers League; his contract-purchase story anchored Ta-Nehisi Coates's 2014 'The Case for Reparations.'

name: Chicago Public Schools
description: Public school district of Chicago (City of Chicago School District #299), established January 5, 1837; the fourth-largest U.S. school district. In 2013 it executed the largest mass school closing in U.S. history, shuttering 50 schools concentrated on the South and West Sides.

name: Congress of Racial Equality (CORE)
description: Interracial civil-rights organization founded in Chicago in 1942 (originally the Committee of Racial Equality) by students tied to the University of Chicago and the Fellowship of Reconciliation; pioneered nonviolent direct action including the first U.S. sit-in (1942), the Freedom Rides (1961), and Freedom Summer (1964).

name: Creator's Way Records
description: Chicago independent record label (active 1990s) that first released Do or Die's 'Po Pimp' (1996), the local hit that drew Rap-A-Lot's attention; the Picture This sessions were partly recorded at Creator's Way Studios in Chicago.

name: Carter G. Woodson Regional Library / Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection
description: Chicago Public Library regional branch at 9525 S. Halsted St. (opened December 19, 1975), named for Carter G. Woodson; permanent home of the Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection of Afro-American History and Literature, the oldest and largest Black history collection in the Midwest.

name: Chicago Metropolitan Mutual Assurance Company
aliases: CMMAC; Chicago Metropolitan Assurance Company; Metropolitan Funeral System Association
description: Chicago Black-owned insurer (1925–1985), subject of Weems's book-length study. Documented case of 'one-way economic desegregation': white firms entered the Black market post-integration, poached Black agents and middle-class customers, and Black insurers — unable to expand their client base — declined nationally from 50 (1962) to 23 (1992).

name: Chicago Area Project
description: Neighborhood-based juvenile delinquency prevention through resident self-organization. Founded in 1934 by University of Chicago sociologist Clifford Shaw; described as America's first community-based delinquency prevention program. Began in the Russell Square neighborhood of South Chicago with a 'bottom up' method: reaching out to gangs and redirecting them into community life rather than punitive control. Works through independent local affiliates (about 40 grassroots organizations and special projects across Chicago and Illinois) using a three-pronged approach of community organizing, direct services, and advocacy.

name: Cook County Bar Association
description: Founded 1914 by Black lawyers (Edward H. Wright, first president; Ida Platt, first Black woman licensed in Illinois, among the founders). The CCBA organized defense of Blacks charged during the 1919 riots — winning acquittals and civil damages — and was honored by the Cook County Board on its 2014 centennial.

name: Chicago Bee Branch Library
aliases: Chicago Bee Library; Chicago Bee Branch (CPL)
description: Chicago Public Library branch at 3647 S State St, operating since 1996 in the renovated former Chicago Bee newspaper building (completed 1931; Chicago Landmark 1998; National Register 1986): Black media infrastructure converted into contemporary neighborhood knowledge infrastructure.

name: Chicago Black United Communities (CBUC)
aliases: CBUC; see-buck; Chicago Black United Communities
description: Black political education and voter-mobilization infrastructure on Chicago's South Side. Founded circa 1980 by Lu Palmer and Jorja Palmer as a nonprofit; began as a coalition of local Black groups and became a membership organization training Black Chicagoans in electoral politics. Ran political education classes modeled on the Black Panther Party's programs under Fred Hampton, in four-week cycles with graduations at which Harold Washington spoke. Trained and deployed some 2,000 organizers; worked with the Urban League, NAACP, and Operation PUSH to register 237,000 new voters (180,000 Black) and raised a near-half-million-dollar war chest, building the constituency that elected Harold Washington mayor in 1983.

name: Chicago Block Clubs / Federation of Block Units and Neighborhood Clubs
aliases: Federation of Block Units and Neighborhood Clubs; Chicago block clubs
description: Block-level resident organizing for sanitation, safety, beautification, and political capacity, originating in Chicago Urban League migrant-orientation work and evolving into a durable Black neighborhood governance tradition. Block clubs organized at the individual block level, coordinated by area councils, and overseen by the Federation of Block Units and Neighborhood Clubs. The League's Community Organisation Department, directed by Alva B. Maxey, strengthened the clubs' structure (1951 annual report; Maxey's 1957 Phylon Quarterly article called the block club the 'natural and popular vehicle' for community cohesion). Federation records dated 1950-1955 are preserved in the Chicago Urban League Records at UIC Library Special Collections.

name: Chicago and Northern District Association of Colored Women's Clubs
aliases: CNDA; City Federation of Colored Women's Clubs; CFCWC
description: Federation of Black women's clubs for Chicago and northern Illinois — an Organization (TYPE CORRECTED 2026-10-06; was mistyped as Venue). Formed in 1906 as the City Federation of Colored Women's Clubs at the organizing of Mrs. Cordelia West (first president) under the motto “From Possibilities to Realities”; incorporated in 1921 under the present name during Irene Gaines's presidency. Sadie L. Adams served as president 1921–1933. The 1921 reorganization brought increased membership, a clubhouse, and a home for dependent children. Member clubs belonged to the Illinois Federation of Colored Women's Clubs. Golden jubilee 1956; diamond jubilee 1981.

name: Cook County Physicians Association
description: Black physicians' professional association founded 1911 in Chicago as the local chapter of the National Medical Association; functions as advocacy body, training pipeline, and scholarship funder.

name: Covenant Bank
description: Faith-capitalized Black community bank on Chicago's West Side (2008-2013); bought from Community Bank of Lawndale by Rev. Bill Winston, funded by thousands of small church-linked shareholders, closed by regulators with deposits assumed by Liberty Bank and Trust.

name: Christmas in Black Chicago
description: Christmas as family-reunion season: Great Migration families spent heavily to travel home or gather kin; distinct food, gifts, worship, and Black Santa imagery; Charlemae Rollins's 1963 anthology 'Christmas Gif'' preserved Black Christmas stories and songs.

name: Chicago Defender / Ebony / Jet advertisements as evidence of Black consumer practice
description: Advertisements in the Chicago-based Black press (Defender 1905–, Ebony 1945–, Jet 1951–) as primary documents of what ordinary Black Chicagoans were being sold and, by inference, were buying: beauty products, cars, food brands, household goods. Also documents who was excluded from mainstream advertising.

name: Corner-store and neighborhood grocery shopping in Black Chicago
description: Everyday grocery procurement in Black neighborhoods across eras: 1930s Black Metropolis residents paying more for lower-quality groceries; the kitchenette economy; postwar corner stores (including Black-owned stores that later sold to immigrant owners); modern food-access gaps and Black-owned markets answering them.

name: Chicago Black social dance culture as everyday lineage — bop to house
description: Umbrella framing practice: Black Chicago social dance as continuous everyday culture — jitterbug → bopping → steppin' → house — transmitted at home by watching parents practice and in neighborhood parties; documented by the Chicago Black Social Culture Map project.

name: Chicago Defender radio and television pages
description: The Defender's broadcast listings, columns, and sponsored programs — a primary source for what Black Chicago could hear/watch and when. (Defender institutional history is sibling project CTL-DR-BPM-003; this entry covers only the broadcast pages as lived-media evidence.)

name: Cadillac (as cultural object)
description: Object biography of the Cadillac marque as a Black cultural symbol: founded 1902 by Henry M. Leland, a GM luxury line from 1909, and — in Black-press discourse — an aspiration to be treated as a 'first class American.' Chuck Berry's Cadillac Eldorado is held by the NMAAHC.

name: City of Chicago MWBE set-aside program (government contracting)
description: Chicago enacted MWBE guidelines in January 1984 and an affirmative-action set-aside program in April 1985 (per trade press, by Harold Washington's executive order), revised it in July 1990 after Croson (25% minority / 5% women-owned goals), and saw the 18-year-old program struck down as not narrowly tailored by Judge James B. Moran on December 29, 2003 in BAGC v. City of Chicago, with a six-month stay for a rewrite.

name: Community Bank of Lawndale / Covenant Bank
description: First Black-owned bank on Chicago's West Side (1977), founded by Rev. Shelvin Jerome Hall; bought in 2008 by Living Word Christian Center with investments from 3,000+ church members and renamed Covenant Bank; closed by regulators 2013.

name: Cottage Grove Avenue commercial corridor (Woodlawn / Chatham)
description: Cottage Grove Avenue is the second major Chatham commercial corridor alongside 79th Street, with a Black-owned culinary node at 75th Street (Lem’s Bar-B-Q, est. 1954; Brown Sugar Bakery, est. 2004; Soul Veg City) and significant transport, including the Cottage Grove Green Line station at 63rd.

name: Chicago Conference on Religion and Race
aliases: CCRR; Chicago Conference on Religion and Race (1963-1984)
description: Interfaith coalition formed immediately following the National Conference on Religion and Race held in Chicago in January 1963. On August 12, 1966, it offered to sponsor a negotiating session between the Chicago Freedom Movement, Mayor Richard J. Daley, business leaders, and real estate officials; the resulting 'Summit Conference' met August 17, 1966 (chaired by Ben Heineman of the Chicago and North Western Railroad) and produced the August 26, 1966 Summit Agreement on fair housing. The agreement charged the CCRR with initiating a continuing metropolitan body. Succeeded by the Council of Religious Leaders of Metropolitan Chicago, created in 1984.

name: Church Mothers
description: The senior women's leadership office in Black Baptist, Methodist, and Sanctified congregations: a recognized moral authority operating alongside (and checking) pastoral authority.

name: Church Program & Choir Anniversary Economy
description: The Black church program economy: choir anniversaries, musicals, and sheet-music sales through church networks that funded and circulated gospel music.

name: Congregational Mutual Aid
description: The sickness-relief, burial, and newcomer-support functions of small congregations: pooled pennies for burial, aid in illness, and migrant reception networks. Documented by Frazier, Lincoln & Mamiya (1990), Butler (1991), Grossman (1989), and Nonprofit Quarterly (2026).

name: Contemporary Storefront Churches (South/West Sides)
description: The living continuation of the storefront tradition on the South and West sides: small, idiosyncratic, neighborhood-embedded congregations documented photographically and journalistically in the 21st century.

name: Coordinating Council of Community Organizations (CCCO)
description: Chicago-based coalition that emerged in 1962 and partnered with SCLC to form the Chicago Freedom Movement. Headquartered at 366 E. 47th Street (the Wells Building); dissolved late 1967.

name: Chong Freeman
description: mother of Marcus Freeman; born in Daegu, South Korea

name: Chris Ash
description: American football coach; defensive coordinator of the Notre Dame Fighting Irish since February 2025. Born December 24, 1973, in Ottumwa, Iowa; played defensive back at Drake University (bachelor's 1996; two-time letterwinner), began coaching as a Drake graduate assistant in 1997, coordinated defenses at Wisconsin, Arkansas, Ohio State (2014 CFP champions) and Texas, was Rutgers head coach 2016-2019, and spent 2024 as a Jacksonville Jaguars scout.

name: Cincinnati Bearcats football
description: Defensive coordinator/linebackers, 2017–2020, under Luke Fickell

name: CULTURETECHLENS NFP
description: Chicago-based 501(c)(3) Black cultural intelligence nonprofit founded by William Maxey; publishes the CultureTechLens Index, an evidence-graded knowledge graph, and open research.

name: Candid
description: Nonprofit information service; CultureTechLens NFP holds its 2026 Gold Seal of Transparency on the Candid profile.

name: Charity Navigator
description: Charity evaluator; lists CULTURETECHLENS NFP (EIN 39-3143901) with verified mission, address, website, and phone.

name: culturetechlens.com
description: Official website of CultureTechLens NFP, launched 2026-09-28; publishes the knowledge graph, the CTL Index, and research.

name: CultureTechLens Index, Edition 2026-10
description: CultureTechLens's monthly cultural-resonance ranking; Edition 2026-10 (Artifacts) deposited on Zenodo 2026-10-05.

name: Coordinating Council of Community Organizations
description: Coalition co-founded by Rev. Arthur M. Brazier and convened by Al Raby; active in the 1966 Chicago Freedom Movement.

name: Cooney Brothers National Theaters Corp
description: The Cooney Brothers National Theaters Corp was the theater company for which Chicago's Stratford Theatre was built. The Stratford, at 715 W. 63rd Street in Englewood, opened on September 4, 1920, with 2,433 seats, presenting vaudeville and movies, and was later operated by Warner Bros. from the 1930s to the 1950s before being torn down. The Cooney circuit also appears in the record as Chicago United Theatres, Inc., owner of record in July 1925 of the Stratford Building — extended to Union Avenue — which sold a 6.5% mortgage bond on the building.

name: Cook County Land Bank Authority
description: The Cook County Land Bank Authority is a public land-bank authority serving Cook County, Illinois. In CultureTechLens research it appears as the public body that took ownership of the vacant Washington Park National Bank Building at 6300 S. Cottage Grove Avenue in Woodlawn, Chicago — a Neoclassical bank building completed in 1924, closed as a bank in 1931, and later used as headquarters of The Woodlawn Organization — acquiring it for equitable, transit-oriented redevelopment. The building was listed among Preservation Chicago's 'Chicago 7' most endangered in 2016 and 2020 and on Landmarks Illinois' Most Endangered list in 2019, and a demolition plan for it was announced in March 2019; its 2026 condition is unconfirmed in the research.

name: City Colleges of Chicago
description: Public community college system operating Kennedy-King College. Stub record.

name: Chicago Conference on Racial Restrictive Covenants (1945)
description: 1945 Chicago strategy conference of lawyers planning the legal attack on racial restrictive covenants; Charles H. Houston spoke.

name: Columbia, South Carolina
description: City in South Carolina; home of the University of South Carolina and Dawn Staley's professional base.

name: Charles H. Houston
description: Civil-rights lawyer; vice-dean of Howard University School of Law; first special counsel to the NAACP; architect of the legal strategy that dismantled Jim Crow.

name: Charlotte Forten
description: Educator and abolitionist; daughter of James Forten.

name: Combahee River Raid
description: June 2, 1863: Union raid up the Combahee River, South Carolina, guided by Harriet Tubman; more than 700 enslaved people freed.

name: Crispus Attucks
description: Sailor and stevedore of African and Native American descent; first person killed in the Boston Massacre (March 5, 1770); 19th-century abolitionist icon.

name: Chicago Philharmonic debut as "Symphony II" (March 1991)
description: First performance of the Orchestral Society of Illinois under the name "Symphony II", led by artistic director Larry Rachleff; the ensemble later renamed the Chicago Philharmonic.

name: Chicago Sister Cities International Program established (1990)
description: Mayor Richard M. Daley's Executive Order 90-1 establishes the Chicago Sister Cities International Program for the benefit of the City of Chicago, its residents, and its businesses.

name: Chicago-Accra sister-city agreement (1989)
description: Sister-city relationship established between Chicago, Illinois and Accra, Ghana.

name: Chicago Freedom Movement activated (January 1966)
description: The SCLC and the CCCO formally activate the Chicago Freedom Movement; Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. moves into a West Side apartment to dramatize the campaign to end slums.

name: Chucho Valdes performs La Creacion at Symphony Center (October 18, 2022)
description: Chucho Valdes performs his four-movement Afro-Cuban suite La Creacion (The Creation) at Symphony Center in Chicago; the work was co-commissioned by the Chicago Symphony Center.

name: Chicago Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events
aliases: DCASE; Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events; Mayor's Office of Special Events
description: City of Chicago department that presents the Chicago Blues Festival and the Chicago Gospel Music Festival (successor in function to the Mayor's Office of Special Events).

name: Chicago Park District
description: Municipal park district of Chicago; John W. Rogers Jr. served as board president for six years in the 1990s.

name: Chicago Police Department
description: Municipal police department of Chicago; Larry Snelling served as superintendent, September 2023–July 2026.

name: Cook County Board of Commissioners
description: Legislature of Cook County, Illinois; Brandon Johnson served as 1st District commissioner, 2018–2023.

name: Chicago Teachers Union
description: Labor union of Chicago public school educators; Brandon Johnson was an organizer from 2012.

name: Chicago Police Board
description: Civilian oversight board for the Chicago Police Department; Lori Lightfoot served as president, 2015–2018.

name: Clergy Alliance (Chicago)
description: Chicago clergy coalition; under Rev. William Lambert it led a selective-buying campaign by Black Chicagoans.

name: Charlotte B. Stratton
description: Black Chicago educator; co-founder (1946) of Howalton Day School — the 'Ton' in the school's name, combined from the founders' surnames.

name: Charles A. Preston
description: Haitian diplomat — a former member of Haiti's diplomatic corps in Washington, D.C. — appointed by the Haitian government as co-commissioner (with Frederick Douglass) to the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition; the two men took possession of and dedicated the Haitian Pavilion on January 2, 1893.

name: Clifton H. Johnson
description: Historian and archivist who founded the Amistad Research Center in 1966 and served as its first administrator and longtime director.

name: Chester Robinson
description: Director of the West Side Organization in 1966. At a press conference he publicly backed the WSO's participation in the march into Cicero over Dr. King's objections, declaring the marchers "a new breed, a new kind of cat without fear."

name: C-SPAN
description: C-SPAN (Cable-Satellite Public Affairs Network) is a nonprofit public-affairs network. In 1997 it bought the license of WDCU, the University of the District of Columbia's 90.1 FM station in Washington, for $13 million, and on October 9, 1997 it launched C-SPAN Radio as WCSP-FM on that frequency. CultureTechLens's preservation research treats the WDCU sale as a warning case for Black cultural assets: the sale came during a financial crisis at the university, the station ceased to exist, and its staff physically carried some 14,000 recordings to safety.

name: Charleston, South Carolina
description: Birthplace of Charlamagne Tha God (Lenard Larry McKelvey, 1978).

name: Cheryl Townsend Gilkes
description: Sociologist of religion whose scholarship documents Black church women’s leadership, including the Church Mothers office.

name: Contract Buyers League founding (1968)
description: The founding of the Contract Buyers League (1968), the North Lawndale organization that fought contract selling.

name: Chandra McCormick
description: New Orleans photographer (born August 28, 1957); artistic partner and wife of Keith Calhoun and co-creator of the Calhoun-McCormick photographic archive; co-founder of the L9 Center for the Arts (2007).

name: Center for Black Music Research
description: Research center founded 1983 at Columbia College Chicago by Samuel A. Floyd Jr. to document, collect, preserve, and disseminate Black music worldwide; target of the 2012 defunding threat.

name: Chicago-L.org
description: Online repository documenting the history of Chicago 'L' stations, including Dorchester station's 1994 Woodlawn debate.

name: Celia Parker Woolley
description: White Unitarian minister and novelist who founded the Frederick Douglass Woman's Club in Chicago in 1906 and, with Ida B. Wells, the Frederick Douglass Center settlement in 1904.

name: ChatBlackGPT
description: Culturally informed AI platform founded by Erin Reddick, providing perspectives from Black and African American communities; launched on Juneteenth 2024.

name: Clarence O. Smith
description: Co-founder of Essence Communications Inc. (1968); with Edward Lewis the majority owner for 35 years; co-visionary of the Essence Music Festival.

name: Caroline Wanga
description: Former Target chief culture, diversity and inclusion officer; joined Essence as Chief Growth Officer in June 2020 and served as interim CEO of Essence Communications from July 2020.

name: California African American Museum
description: Museum in Los Angeles, California; hosted the June 19, 2015 news conference announcing the Freedmen's Bureau Project.

name: Columbus, Ohio
description: City in Ohio; birthplace of Granville T. Woods (April 23, 1856), where he attended school until age 10.

name: Chicago Transit Authority
description: Owner and operator of Chicago's 'L' system, including the Green Line and Halsted station.

name: Clarence Ludd
description: Owner of the High Chaparral, the South Side soul club at 7740 South Stony Island Avenue near 79th Street, one of Chicago's most popular Black clubs of the 1960s and 1970s.

name: Clifton F. Richardson Sr.
aliases: Clifton Frederick Richardson Sr.; Clifton Richardson
description: Black editor, publisher, journalist, and civic activist in Houston (1911-1939); founded the Houston Observer (1916, with partners), the Houston Informer (1919), and the Houston Defender (1930); founding member of the Civic Betterment League of Harris County and later president of Houston's NAACP chapter.

name: Carol Ammons
description: Illinois State Representative (D-Urbana); elected Joint Chairwoman of the Illinois Legislative Black Caucus in January 2023.

name: Clarence Jones
description: Attorney and former publisher of the New York Amsterdam News; close associate of Martin Luther King Jr.; co-led the 1970 founding of Inner City Broadcasting Corporation.

name: Chicago Council of Negro Organizations
description: Coalition founded in 1939 by Irene McCoy Gaines to protest education inequality and segregation; coordinated nearly 100 civic, educational, religious, and labor organizations.

name: Chicago Tribune
description: Chicago daily newspaper; Roi Ottley was a columnist there in the early 1950s.

name: Chicago Fire Department
description: Municipal fire department of Chicago; Larry Langford served as its Director of Media Affairs and Communications 2000-2025, retiring after 25 years.

name: Cambridge, Massachusetts
description: City whose voter list Latanya Sweeney bought from City Hall for $25 for her 1997 re-identification experiment.

name: Chelsea, Massachusetts
description: City in Massachusetts; birthplace of inventor Lewis Howard Latimer (born September 4, 1848); his parents, formerly enslaved, had fled to freedom there.

name: Collaboraction Theatre Company
description: Collaboraction Theatre Company (also recorded as Collaboraction) is a Chicago theater company devoted to social-issue-driven contemporary theater. Its documented mainstage work in the evidence corpus is the 2019–20 season, staged at the Kennedy-King College theaters in Englewood — the U Building's 292-seat mainstage and black box theaters at 740 W. 63rd Street. The Kennedy-King College theaters' graph record names that season 'We Are Each Other's Business,' including the fourth annual Peacebook Festival and the 'Red Island' world premiere, and places it as year three of Collaboraction's five-year One City plan. The graph record's era is 2019–2020 and its status Verified, resting on a single BroadwayWorld season announcement; the underlying place research graded the same BroadwayWorld item as press-release-style when auditing the venue record.

name: Claude Lightfoot
description: Prominent Black communist for almost 60 years. The FBI's Chicago field office held 24 volumes (almost 5,000 pages) on him; they were destroyed in the 2013 Alexandria archives flood.

name: CMT.com archive wipe (June 2024)
description: Paramount Global removed CMT.com's website archives in the same June 2024 sweep that deleted MTVNews.com; content redirected to the main MTV site.

name: Chris Morrow
description: Co-founder and CEO of the Loud Speakers Network. Former Director of Urban Programming for Premiere Radio Networks (iHeart's syndication arm); previously a writer who entered podcasting as a hobby. Met Reggie Ossé on Twitter c.2010 and built LSN from The Combat Jack Show.

name: Chicago Collections
description: Consortium of Chicago-area libraries, museums, and institutions with archives that collaborate to preserve and share the history and culture of the Chicago region; formed as an LLC in 2012. Its EXPLORE digital portal launched October 2015.

name: C.D. Murray
description: African-American barber; founder of Murray's Superior Products Co. in 1925, first selling his heavy-hold waxy pomade from his Chicago barbershop.

name: Charles S. Johnson
description: Charles Spurgeon Johnson (1893-1956): sociologist; established the National Urban League's research department (1921); founded and edited Opportunity (1923-1928); first Black president of Fisk University (1946-1956).

name: Christopher J. Perry Sr.
description: Baltimore-born Black journalist who founded the Philadelphia Tribune in 1884 and led it until his death in 1921.

name: Chicago Defender ends print edition (2019)
description: Final print edition of the Chicago Defender published July 10, 2019; the paper continued as an online-only publication under publisher Real Times Media.

name: CNN
description: American cable news network; Roland Martin was a contributor for six years (2007-2013).

name: Candy
description: Jackie Ormes's single-panel cartoon about an attractive, wisecracking housemaid; ran in the Chicago Defender for four months in 1945.

name: Charli D'Amelio
description: TikTok creator whose uncredited 2019–2020 posts of the Renegade dance drew millions of views; later collaborated with Jalaiah Harmon and credited her.

name: Consolidated Lasting Machine Company
description: Company formed in 1889 to manufacture Jan Matzeliger's lasting machines; Matzeliger retained substantial ownership.

name: Channel F
description: Fairchild Channel F (1976): first home video game console to use interchangeable game cartridges; developed by Jerry Lawson's team from an Alpex prototype.

name: Colorado Buffaloes football
description: University of Colorado football program (Boulder); Mel Tucker was head coach for the 2019 season before Michigan State hired him in February 2020.

name: Cleveland Browns
description: NFL franchise (Cleveland, Ohio); Mel Tucker was defensive backs coach 2005-2007 and defensive coordinator in 2008, when the Browns ranked second in the NFL with 23 interceptions.

name: Cold Chillin' Records
description: Hip-hop record label founded in 1986; Marley Marl served as its in-house producer, and it was home to many Juice Crew artists.

name: Cleveland, Ohio
description: City in northeastern Ohio; Mel Tucker was born there on January 4, 1972, and attended Cleveland Heights High School.

name: Coretta Scott King
description: American civil rights activist (Apr 27, 1927 - Jan 30, 2006); wife of Martin Luther King Jr. (m. 1953). Antioch College 1951; New England Conservatory of Music voice degree 1954. Subject of Moneta Sleet Jr.'s 1969 Pulitzer-winning photograph.

name: Columbia University
description: University whose data-journalism master's program Sherrell Dorsey completed; Dorsey's reporting has appeared in the Columbia Journalism Review.

name: Carson Products
description: Carson Products was a Black-owned hair-care firm. In 1988 it merged with Soft Sheen to form SoftSheen-Carson — a consolidation Black Enterprise chronicled in its June 1989 '45 Great Moments' series, in the entry on the Jheri Curl trend pushing Soft Sheen. A decade later, in 1998, the Gardner family sold the combined SoftSheen-Carson to L'Oréal of Paris. The sale's meaning for Black business ownership remained contested a generation later: WAMC revisited it in 2014 under the title 'A Black Cosmetic Company Sells, Or Sells Out?'

name: Charlotte
description: North Carolina city where Sherrell Dorsey ran BLKTECHCLT (first hub for 2,000+ entrepreneurs and technologists of color) and worked on Google Fiber's launch sales team.

name: Clarence Page
description: Columnist and editorial board member, Chicago Tribune. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Chicago Tribune Post-Election Panel' (2012-11-15).

name: Candice Jones
description: Executive Director, Illinois Juvenile Justice Commission. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Juvenile Justice in Cook County: The View from Inside' (2016-06-01).

name: Charles Thomas
description: Political reporter, WLS-TV ABC 7 Chicago. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program '2016 Primary Election Analysis' (2016-03-17).

name: Cecilia Conrad
description: Managing Director, MacArthur Foundation (MacArthur Fellows Program). Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Inspiring Creativity: 35 Years of the MacArthur Fellows Program' (2016-01-12).

name: Charles Lee Isbell Jr.
description: 11th Chancellor, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (took office July 2025). Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Charles Lee Isbell Jr., Chancellor, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign' (2026-01-08).

name: Clayton Harris III
description: Candidate for Cook County State's Attorney; Lecturer, University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy. Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Clayton Harris III' (2024-03-07).

name: Cleopatra Pendleton
description: Founder, Hadiya's Promise; mother of Hadiya Pendleton (panelist). Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Chicago's Homicide Crisis' (2016-06-20).

name: Ciere Boatright
description: Commissioner, Chicago Department of Planning and Development (appointed Nov 2023) (headliner). Appeared at City Club of Chicago program 'Ciere Boatright, Commissioner, Chicago Department of Planning & Development, in conversation with Dan Gibbons, CEO, City Club Chicago' (2025-06-25).

name: Charles Mingus
description: Charles Mingus was a bassist, pianist, composer, and bandleader, one of the jazz artists documented in the National Postal Museum's “African Americans in Jazz” exhibit on Black history postage stamps (Smithsonian, via Google Arts & Culture).

name: Charlie Parker
description: Charlie Parker was a saxophonist and composer who helped develop bebop. His Chicago footprint is documented in CultureTechLens research. On October 23, 1950, Parker played the Pershing Ballroom, at Cottage Grove Avenue and 64th Street in Woodlawn, a performance preserved as a live recording documented by its LP liner notes; CTL's CTL-DR-ECON-001 timeline likewise records him playing the Pershing Ballroom, part of the Pershing Hotel complex on 63rd Street, in 1950. An earlier Chicago association — Parker's place in the Dream Band at Bronzeville's Rhumboogie Café in the 1940s — is carried in CTL research as provisional, pending verification against period press.

In CultureTechLens research she is documented on a Chicago stage at the height of the South Side theater era: Chicago Defender citations preserved in University of Chicago guide research record Ahmad Jamal, Cannonball Adderley, and Carmen McRae at the Tivoli Theatre, the Balaban & Katz movie palace at 63rd Street and Cottage Grove Avenue, on December 31, 1959.

name: Carmen Lundy
description: Carmen Lundy is a jazz vocalist, composer, educator, and visual artist, and a recipient of the National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Masters Fellowship for 2026. Her fellowship is documented directly by the NEA's own honors pages — the basis on which the CTL-JAZZ-100 collection grades her record Verified, in contrast to the collection's many fellowship years taken from Wikipedia's secondary roster. She is entry CTL-JAZZ-099 in the collection of 100 African American jazz artists (2026). No further biographical passage about her exists in the corpus.

name: Chicago Smart Communities
description: Chicago Smart Communities is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as an Event, Provisional, under project TECH-001. Its cited source, the research brief 'Black Chicago Goes Online' (CTL-RB-TECH-000002 v1.0, 2026-10-09), states that nine Chicago community areas joined the MacArthur-backed Digital Excellence Demonstration Communities initiative in 2009, and that a $7 million federal broadband grant funded the Chicago Smart Communities program in 2010, rolling out that October. Estimated home broadband in the nine areas rose from 47 percent in 2008 to 56 percent in 2011, while the rest of the city went from 64 to 70 percent. Only three of the nine areas are majority Black — Englewood, West Englewood, and Auburn Gresham — with mixed results: West Englewood gained an estimated 28 points, Auburn Gresham 18, Englewood stayed flat. The brief's analysis: the areas gained faster but started far lower, so the gap narrowed without closing.

name: Chicago Connected
description: Chicago Connected is a Chicago broadband-access program launched in 2020 to provide free broadband to qualifying Chicago Public Schools families. Its reach grew past 100,000 students by 2022 — the figure documented in Kids First Chicago's 2020–2022 Impact Report — and past 200,000 students by 2025. It is recorded in CultureTechLens's 'Black Chicago Goes Online' research (CTL-RB-TECH-000002), with underlying citations to Kids First Chicago and the City of Chicago, and its graph record remains Provisional.

name: Channing Crowder
description: Former NFL linebacker who played his entire six-season career (2005-2010) with the Miami Dolphins after an All-American career at Florida; co-host of The Pivot Podcast.

name: Corey Holcomb
description: Corey Holcomb (full name Corey Lamont Holcomb) is a Chicago-born comedian, radio host, and actor, recorded in the CultureTechLens graph under project MEDIA-001 with a Provisional verification status and an era of 1990s–present. He is the host of The Corey Holcomb 5150 Show, which the record describes as airing live on YouTube on Tuesday nights. The record rests on three non-primary sources viewed on 2026-10-11: a Google creator profile for @coreyholcomb5150land, the Wikipedia article on Corey Holcomb linked from that profile, and an informationcradle.com facts page covering his date of birth and roles. No passage in the research corpus or the build files documents his act, credits, or career beyond this record, and none is added here.

name: Cesar Chavez
aliases: Cesar Estrada Chavez; Cesario Estrada Chavez
description: Cesar Estrada Chavez (March 31, 1927, near Yuma, Arizona — April 23, 1993, San Luis, Arizona) was a Mexican American farm-labor leader who, after migrant field work and service in the U.S. Navy, organized with the Community Service Organization from 1952 before co-founding the National Farm Workers Association with Dolores Huerta in 1962. That association became the United Farm Workers, and Chavez led its nonviolent strikes, boycotts, marches, and fasts, including the Delano grape strike of 1965–1970, the 1966 march to Sacramento, and a 25-day fast in 1968 that drew a supportive telegram from Martin Luther King Jr. Growers signed contracts in 1970, and California passed the Agricultural Labor Relations Act in 1975. In March 2026, a New York Times investigation reported allegations that Chavez sexually abused women and girls, including Huerta; he was never charged, died in 1993, and cannot answer them, and institutions have since renamed commemorations — a reckoning this record states plainly alongside the labor history.

name: Claudette Colvin
description: Claudette Colvin was a Montgomery schoolgirl whose refusal, at fifteen, to surrender her bus seat to a white passenger on March 2, 1955, came nine months before Rosa Parks's famous arrest in the same city and the same bus system. Dragged from the bus, handcuffed, and jailed, she had been studying Black history at school and later recalled feeling held in her seat by the examples of earlier freedom fighters. Movement leaders, weighing her youth and circumstances, chose Parks as the public face of protest, and Colvin's name faded from popular memory for decades. Her courage, however, entered the legal record directly: she became one of the four plaintiffs in Browder v. Gayle, the federal case that ended segregated bus seating in Montgomery, affirmed by the Supreme Court in 1956. She later moved to New York, worked for decades as a nurse's aide, raised a family largely out of the spotlight, and saw her juvenile record expunged in 2021. Recognition arrived late but fully, through biography, honors, and renewed teaching of her story. Colvin died in Texas on January 13, 2026, aged eighty-six, and this record is written in tribute: the teenager the movement set aside was, in the end, one of its decisive witnesses.
