name: Cory Booker
description: Cory Anthony Booker (born April 27, 1969, in Washington, D.C., and raised in Harrington Park, New Jersey) is the United States senator from New Jersey. A Stanford and Yale Law graduate and Rhodes Scholar, he entered politics on Newark's Municipal Council (1998–2002) and served as the city's mayor from 2006 to 2013, presiding over a much-watched attempt to revive New Jersey's largest city. When Senator Frank Lautenberg died in office, Booker won the October 16, 2013, special election and was sworn in on October 31, 2013 — the first Black senator in New Jersey's history. He sought the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and became a national figure again on March 31–April 1, 2025, when he held the Senate floor for twenty-five hours and five minutes, the longest speech in the chamber's recorded history, breaking the mark Strom Thurmond set filibustering the Civil Rights Act of 1957 — a record Booker, a Black senator from the movement's own tradition, surpassed by forty-seven minutes. With Scott, Warnock, Blunt Rochester, and Alsobrooks, he completes the five — the most Black senators ever to serve at once.

name: Colin Powell
description: Colin Luther Powell (born April 5, 1937, in Harlem, New York, to Jamaican immigrant parents) rose through the United States Army from a City College ROTC commission to four-star general and the summit of American military and diplomatic office. He served two tours in Vietnam, then climbed the national-security ladder: National Security Advisor to President Reagan from 1987 to 1989 — the first Black American in that post — and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff from 1989 to 1993, the first Black officer and the youngest person to hold the military's highest office, presiding over the Panama invasion and the Gulf War. On January 20, 2001 — the date the intake timeline files for him — Powell was sworn in as Secretary of State under President George W. Bush, the first Black American to hold that office, serving through the September 11 attacks and the opening of the Iraq War, whose case he presented to the United Nations in February 2003 and later called a lasting blot on his record. He died on October 18, 2021. The audit found no trace of him in the graph; this record corrects the absence.

name: Cyrus Colter
description: Cyrus Colter (January 8, 1910 – April 15, 2002) was a Chicago lawyer, public servant, and fiction writer who began publishing at fifty and became one of the city's most exacting chroniclers of Black working- and middle-class life. Born in Noblesville, Indiana, he moved to Chicago in 1936 to study law at Chicago-Kent College of Law, graduating in 1940; he served as an Army captain in Italy in World War II and sat on the Illinois Commerce Commission for twenty-three years. His story collection The Beach Umbrella (1970) won the University of Iowa School of Letters' first prize for short fiction. Novels followed — The River of Eros (1972), The Hippodrome (1973), and the widely praised A Chocolate Soldier (1988). In 1973 he joined Northwestern University's faculty, and in 1976 he became the first African American to hold an endowed chair there, as Chester D. Tripp Professor in the Humanities. He died in 2002, aged ninety-two.

name: Cazzie Russell
description: Cazzie Lee Russell (born June 7, 1944, in Chicago) is the Chicago-born forward who starred at Carver High School, built a legend at the University of Michigan, and played twelve NBA seasons. At Carver he was the Chicago Sun-Times Boys' Player of the Year and Mr. Basketball USA in 1962. At Michigan (1963–66) he scored 2,163 points, averaged a school-record 27.1 points per game, won three consecutive Big Ten titles, and was named national college player of the year in 1966; the Wolverines' Crisler Arena is still called “the House That Cazzie Built,” and Michigan retired his No. 33 in 1989. Drafted first overall by the New York Knicks in 1966, he won the 1970 NBA championship, earned an All-Star selection in 1972, and closed his playing career with the Chicago Bulls in 1977–78. He then coached for more than four decades, and current listings (checked October 2026) show him as an assistant coach at Flagler College. Russell is living, and this record is written as a living-subject record.

name: Cliff Kelley
aliases: Clifford Kelley; Governor of Talk Radio
description: Cliff Kelley is a Chicago talk-radio host and former 20th Ward alderman whose quarter-century as a WVON host made him, in the words of a 2019 United States Senate tribute, the 'Governor of Talk Radio.' A native of Chicago's South Side, he graduated from Englewood High School, Roosevelt University, and the John Marshall Law School. Before radio he served 16 years as alderman of the 20th Ward and as an elected school board member; the Senate tribute credits him as an early champion of racial equality and of LGBTQ rights. Kelley hosted a daily WVON talk show for 25 years — then-State Senator Barack Obama was among those who guest-hosted in his absence — and in March 2019 stepped down from the daily program while continuing a weekly American Heroes show for veterans, a community-ambassador role, and fill-in hosting. Editor & Publisher has called him 'the most influential talk radio host in Black Chicago.'

name: Cosmopolitan Church of Prayer
aliases: Cosmopolitan Church of Prayer of Chicago; Cosmo
description: Cosmopolitan Church of Prayer is a South Side Chicago congregation founded on April 29, 1959, by gospel singer and pastor Dr. Charles G. Hayes, beginning in the basement of a home at 634 Woodland Park. Gospel historian Robert M. Marovich counts it among the first Chicago churches to adopt the new Detroit gospel choral style. The congregation grew through a Cottage Grove Avenue storefront and, from 1961, a converted post office on South Langley Avenue, before settling at 842 East 65th Street in Woodlawn, the corner of 65th and Maryland the church calls "Love Corner." Its choir, the Warriors, became one of the most successful recording and radio church choirs in gospel history, releasing more than thirty albums and carrying Hayes's Sunday-night broadcasts; signature recordings include "Jesus Can Work It Out" and "Step Back, Let God Do It."

name: Christian Tabernacle Church
aliases: Christian Tabernacle Church of Chicago; Christian Tabernacle Baptist Church
description: Christian Tabernacle Church is a Chicago congregation founded by the Rev. Maceo Woods at 47th Street and Prairie Avenue in the Grand Boulevard neighborhood; the church's own site gives its address as 4712 S. Prairie Ave. Woods founded the church in 1959, after serving as music minister at Hyde Park Bible Church, and the congregation grew from a founding handful to more than 800 members within its first year; its 60th anniversary was marked in 2019. Its choir — the Christian Tabernacle Concert Choir — became one of Chicago gospel's signature recording ensembles, releasing albums with Woods for Vee-Jay, Volt/Stax's Gospel Truth line, Savoy, and Arista across five decades, including Hello Sunshine (1970), recorded live at the church. In the early 1960s the church's gospel programming brought Detroit's Rev. C. L. Franklin to Chicago, with his daughter Aretha Franklin singing. Woods pastored the church until his death on January 11, 2020; the congregation continues at the Prairie Avenue address.

name: Club Shay Shay
description: Club Shay Shay is an interview podcast and video series hosted by former NFL tight end Shannon Sharpe, launched in the fall of 2020 and produced with The Volume and Sharpe's own Shay Shay Media. Built around long-form conversations with athletes, entertainers, and public figures, it became one of the most-watched interview shows in American sports media, taped in Sharpe's clubhouse-style set. Its January 3, 2024 interview with comedian Katt Williams drew more than 26 million views within 72 hours and, by The Hollywood Reporter's account, roughly 63 million views within two months alongside 1.7 million audio downloads; GQ later reported the episode at about 83 million views. Sharpe has said the episode earned him more than any single season of his NFL career. The show spawned the Nightcap series, staged alongside it in this packet. Club Shay Shay itself had no CultureTechLens record before this packet, though CultureTechLens published a Short on it in October 2026 — the reverse gap closed here.

name: Craig Robinson
description: Craig Robinson — the basketball coach and Michelle Obama's older brother, not the comedian of the same name — is an American college basketball coach and administrator, born in 1962 in Chicago, Illinois, the son of Fraser Robinson, a Chicago Water Department worker, and Marian Robinson, a secretary and homemaker. He grew up in the Euclid Park neighborhood on the South Side and starred at Mount Carmel High School. At Princeton University he became a two-time first-team All-Ivy League selection, was the Ivy League's leading scorer in 1982 and 1983, and finished as Princeton's fourth-leading scorer of all time. After earning degrees in economics at Princeton and an MBA at the University of Chicago, he worked ten years in bond trading and investment management in Chicago. Basketball pulled him back: after assisting at Northwestern, he head coached at Brown University (2006–2008) and Oregon State University (2008–2014). He later served as a New York Knicks player-development executive and as executive director of the National Association of Basketball Coaches from 2020.

name: Cory Hardrict
description: Cory Hardrict (born November 9, 1979) is an American actor from Chicago, Illinois, who built a three-decade screen career from guest television roles in the 1990s to leading film parts. Raised on the South Side and a graduate of Bloom Trail High School, he relocated to Los Angeles and appeared on series including Smart Guy, Felicity, Once and Again, ER, CSI: Miami, and Cold Case. His film work includes Never Been Kissed (1999), Crazy/Beautiful (2001), Gran Torino (2008), Battle: Los Angeles (2011), Warm Bodies (2013), and American Sniper (2014). He portrayed Haitian Jack in the Tupac biopic All Eyez on Me (2017) and starred as Dante in Tyler Perry's Divorce in the Black (2024), a breakout role his own interviews trace to his lived experience. He co-founded the production company Hardcor Films and has produced independent features including Connescence in 2024. Long cast as a dependable supporting player, Hardrict's recent leading roles and producer work mark a second act built on persistence and Chicago-rooted screen craft.

name: Children of Blood and Bone (2027 film)
description: Children of Blood and Bone is a Paramount Pictures fantasy film directed by Gina Prince-Bythewood, who co-wrote the screenplay with Tomi Adeyemi from Adeyemi's 2018 debut novel. Set in the kingdom of Orïsha, it follows Zélie, played by Thuso Mbedu, on a quest to restore the magic violently taken from her people, alongside her brother Tzain (Tosin Cole) and the royal siblings Amari (Amandla Stenberg) and Inan (Damson Idris). The ensemble includes Chiwetel Ejiofor as King Saran, Cynthia Erivo, Lashana Lynch, Idris Elba, Regina King and Viola Davis. Paramount released the first trailer in July 2026, and the cast and filmmakers presented the film at New York Comic Con on October 10, 2026, in a panel moderated by Rian Johnson. The film is scheduled for theatrical release on January 15, 2027, including IMAX engagements. CultureTechLens covered the Comic Con presentation in Short #145, published October 14, 2026.

name: Corey Maggette
description: Corey Maggette, born Corey A. Maggette on November 12, 1979, in Melrose Park, Illinois, is an American former professional basketball player and broadcaster. At Fenwick High School in Oak Park — where his No. 50 jersey is retired — he averaged 23 points and 10 rebounds per game, earned All-State honors, and was named a McDonald's All-American in 1998. After one season at Duke, reaching the 1999 NCAA championship game, he was selected 13th overall in the 1999 NBA draft by the Seattle SuperSonics and traded to the Orlando Magic. Maggette played fourteen NBA seasons, eight of them with the Los Angeles Clippers (2000–2008), built on a relentless foul-drawing attacking style, followed by Golden State, Milwaukee, Charlotte, and a final season with the Detroit Pistons (2012–2013). He totaled 13,198 points in 827 games. He later won a BIG3 league MVP award, worked as a Clippers broadcaster and NBA analyst, and has run the Maggette Basketball Academy youth program for a decade.

name: Chicago American Gears
description: The Chicago American Gears were a Chicago professional basketball team owned by Maurice White and named for his American Gear & Manufacturing Company, which played in the National Basketball League from 1944 to 1947 after an amateur season in the AAU. The Gears are remembered for one season: in 1946–47, after a weeks-long contract holdout, DePaul University star George Mikan joined the team late, played 25 games at 16.5 points per game, and led playoff upsets of the Indianapolis Kautskys, the Oshkosh All-Stars and the Rochester Royals to win the 1947 NBL championship — then widely considered the most prestigious title in professional basketball. White then withdrew the team from the NBL to launch his own Professional Basketball League of America, which collapsed during its first season in 1947; the Gears folded with it, and a dispersal process sent Mikan to the Minneapolis Lakers. George Mikan's record (CTL-E-5543) has named this team as a mint candidate since the Named Queues packet; this record gives his Chicago championship a home in the graph.

name: Cheryl Burton
description: Cheryl Burton, born Cheryl Annette Burton on December 25, 1962, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American television news anchor. A graduate of Lindblom Technical High School (1980), she earned a B.S. in psychology and biology from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1984. After early television work that included Romper Room, Star Search, and her own cable program Simply Elegant, and two years teaching special education, she joined WGN-TV in 1989 as co-anchor of MBR: The Minority Business Report, then worked at WMBD in Peoria and KWCH in Wichita. Burton joined WLS-TV, Chicago's ABC 7, in November 1992 as a weekend co-anchor and reporter, and was promoted in 2003 to co-anchor of the 5 p.m. newscast and contributing anchor at 10 p.m. Her honors include the National Association of Black Journalists Salute to Excellence International Award in 2008 and induction, as its first alumnus so honored, into the Lindblom High School Hall of Fame in 2007.

name: Chloe Bailey
description: Chloe Bailey, born Chloe Elizabeth Bailey on 1 July 1998 in Atlanta, Georgia, is an American singer and actress who records solo as Chlöe. With her younger sister Halle she formed the duo Chloe x Halle, whose viral YouTube covers of Beyoncé songs led to a signing with Beyoncé's Parkwood label; Bailey produced or co-produced most of the duo's material. Their albums The Kids Are Alright (2018) and Ungodly Hour (2020) were both Grammy-nominated, and the duo holds five Grammy nominations since 2018. Bailey acted as Jazz Forster in Grown-ish before launching solo with "Have Mercy" (2021), the album In Pieces (31 March 2023) and Trouble in Paradise (9 August 2024). name: Central Cee
description: Central Cee, born Oakley Neil Caesar-Su on 4 June 1998 in Ladbroke Grove, London, England, and raised in Shepherd's Bush, is a British rapper who carried UK drill to a global audience. His father is of Guyanese and Chinese ancestry and his mother is English, per sourced interview-based reporting — the heritage this record documents as his line into the Black British music story the graph tells. He broke through in 2020 with "Day in the Life" and "Loading"; the mixtapes Wild West (2021, UK No. 2) and 23 (2022, UK No. 1) followed, and "Doja" (2022) reached UK No. 2. "Sprinter," with Dave, spent ten consecutive weeks at UK No. 1 in 2023, then the longest-running UK rap No. 1. Signed to Columbia in June 2023, his debut album Can't Rush Greatness (24 January 2025) hit UK No. 1 and US No. 9 — the first UK rap album to reach the US top ten.

name: Chrisean Rock
description: Chrisean Rock, born Chrisean Eugenia Malone on 14 March 2000 in West Baltimore, Maryland, is an American reality-television personality and recording artist, one of twelve siblings and a former track athlete who attended Santa Monica College. She won Fox's Ultimate Tag in 2020 and rose through Blueface's Blue Girls Club, signing to his BluefaceLLC label; her debut single "Lonely," with Blueface, appeared in 2020, followed by "Vibe." She became a central cast member of Zeus Network's Baddies across four seasons (2022–2026) and of Blueface & Chrisean: Crazy in Love (2022–2023). In 2025 she pivoted publicly toward gospel music, performing the single "Yahweh" live at Faith City Central in Brandywine, Maryland, on 30 March 2025. Her notability rests primarily on reality television rather than a chart-established recording career, and no Billboard chart peak was sourced for her music.

name: Carver High School
aliases: George Washington Carver Area High School; George Washington Carver Military Academy; Carver Military Academy
description: Carver High School — today the George Washington Carver Military Academy — is a public Chicago high school at 13100 South Doty Avenue in the Riverdale area of the city's Far South Side, operated by Chicago Public Schools and named for scientist and educator George Washington Carver. The district established the school in 1947 to serve the families of the Altgeld Gardens housing development, which had opened nearby in 1944, and the school opened its doors on January 4, 1949, with 875 students. It is now a public four-year military high school whose teams, the Challengers, compete in the Chicago Public League. Carver's place in this graph is its basketball line: it is the high school of Cazzie Russell, the Chicago Sun-Times Boys' Player of the Year and Mr. Basketball USA in 1962, and of Tim Hardaway Sr., whose jersey the school retired in 2022. A building at the current address was completed in 1973, with renovations finished in 1995. Chicago Public Schools reporting gives enrollment of 397 students for 2022–23.

name: Cincinnati Tigers
description: The Cincinnati Tigers were a professional Negro league baseball club based in Cincinnati, Ohio, founded in 1934 by DeHart Hubbard, the first African American to win an individual Olympic gold medal (the long jump at the 1924 Paris Games). Built from Hubbard's Excelsior amateur club, the Tigers played in the integrated Indiana-Ohio League and the Negro Southern League before joining the new Negro American League as charter members in 1937, which raised the club to major-league status. The Tigers played at Crosley Field, home of the Cincinnati Reds, and wore the Reds' cast-off uniforms. Managed in 1937 by Ted "Double Duty" Radcliffe, the club finished second in the league's overall standings and sent five players — Radcliffe, Howard Easterling, Ducky Davenport, Porter Moss, and Rainey Bibbs — to the East-West All-Star Game. The club folded after its single major-league season; one Cincinnati account holds that the team was sold and became the Memphis Red Sox, a lineage claim this record reports rather than asserts.

name: Chuck D
aliases: Carlton Douglas Ridenhour; Mistachuck; Carl Ryder
description: Chuck D, born Carlton Douglas Ridenhour on August 1, 1960, in New York, is an American rapper best known as the leader and frontman of Public Enemy, the group he co-founded in 1985 with Flavor Flav. He studied graphic design at Adelphi University on Long Island and worked at the campus radio station WBAU, where a recording of 'Public Enemy No. 1' reached Def Jam co-founder Rick Rubin and led to the group's signing. His baritone delivery and politically charged writing helped create politically and socially conscious hip-hop in the mid-1980s, on albums including It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back (1988) and Fear of a Black Planet (1990). The Source ranked him No. 12 on its list of the Top 50 Hip-Hop Lyricists of All Time. He released the solo album Autobiography of Mistachuck in 1996, later performed with the supergroup Prophets of Rage, and founded the Rapstation platform. As a member of Public Enemy he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2013 and received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award, alongside six career Grammy nominations. Public Enemy itself holds a record in this graph (CTL-E-5699); this record is the frontman endpoint its member wiring was missing.

name: Colin Cowherd
description: Colin Cowherd (born Colin Murray Cowherd on January 6, 1964) is an American sports broadcaster raised in Grayland, Washington, and the founder of the podcast network The Volume (CTL-E-5706). He began as the play-by-play voice of the Las Vegas Stars, the San Diego Padres' Triple-A affiliate, and became sports director at KVBC in Las Vegas, where he was named Nevada Sportscaster of the Year five times; anchor stops in Tampa and Portland followed, and in Portland his radio program The Herd took shape. He joined ESPN Radio in the early 2000s, and The Herd with Colin Cowherd became one of the network's most popular programs; he also co-hosted ESPN's SportsNation from 2009 to 2012 and wrote the New York Times bestseller You HERD Me! (2013). In 2015 he left ESPN for FOX Sports and iHeartMedia, relaunching The Herd on FS1 and FOX Sports Radio. On February 1, 2021, The Volume launched with iHeartMedia as partner and his own Colin Cowherd Podcast as its flagship; the Sports Business Journal's company profile lists Cowherd as the network's founder. He was inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame in 2025.

name: Caleb McLaughlin
description: Caleb McLaughlin, born Caleb Reginald McLaughlin on 13 October 2001 and raised in Carmel, New York, is an American actor who began on Broadway and became a defining face of streaming-era television. Trained in dance at the Harlem School of the Arts under former Lion King producer Aubrey Lynch, he played young Simba in The Lion King on Broadway from 2012 to 2014, taking small television roles alongside the run. In 2016 he was cast as Lucas Sinclair in Netflix's Stranger Things, a role he held through the series' final season in 2025; the cast won the Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series. He played the young Ricky Bell in BET's miniseries The New Edition Story (2017), appeared in Steven Soderbergh's High Flying Bird (2019), and took his first lead role in a feature film in Concrete Cowboy (2020). Voice work in animation, including Final Space and Summer Camp Island, rounds out a career built, unusually, on two long-running ensembles: a Broadway musical and a global streaming phenomenon that grew up alongside its young cast.

name: Carla Jeffery
description: Carla Jeffery, born 10 July 1993 in Houston, Texas, was an American actress who began performing at age twelve, playing a younger version of Mo'Nique's character in the comedy Phat Girlz (2006). She held a recurring role as Keysha Black on HBO's Curb Your Enthusiasm (2007–2009) and built a steady run of television work before her defining role as Bree, the Seabrook High cheerleader and best friend of Addison, in Disney Channel's Zombies (2018). She returned as Bree in Zombies 2 (2020) and Zombies 3 (2022) and voiced the character in Zombies: The Re-Animated Series (2024). name: Carter Bryant
description: Carter Bryant, born Carter Dayne Bryant on 26 November 2005 in Riverside, California, is an American forward for the San Antonio Spurs. He grew up in a bilingual, bicultural household: his father, D'Cean Bryant, is African American, played college basketball at Long Beach State and later coached him in high school, and his mother, Sabrina Torres, is Latina and works as a sign-language interpreter; both of his maternal grandparents are deaf, and his grandfather is in the USA Deaf Basketball Hall of Fame. Bryant has said in his own words that he tries to represent the Latino community, the deaf community, Riverside and the African-American community alike. A McDonald's All-American at Corona Centennial, he played one season at the University of Arizona, averaging 6.5 points and 4.1 rebounds, and San Antonio selected him 14th overall in the 2025 NBA draft. As a rookie he played a reserve role for the Spurs, competed in the 2026 Slam Dunk Contest and won the 2026 Rising Stars Challenge, and he was on San Antonio's roster through the October 2026 preseason. He is not related to Kobe Bryant; reporting on his family background states there is no family connection between them.

name: CeeDee Lamb
description: CeeDee Lamb, born Cedarian DeLeon Lamb on 8 April 1999 in Opelousas, Louisiana, is an American football wide receiver for the Dallas Cowboys. His family relocated to the Houston area after Hurricane Katrina, and he starred at Foster High School in Richmond, Texas, before playing at the University of Oklahoma, where he was a consensus All-American in 2019. Dallas selected him 17th overall in the 2020 NFL Draft and gave him the franchise's storied No. 88 jersey. He has been selected to the Pro Bowl in five of his first six seasons. His peak year to date was 2023, when he led the NFL with 135 receptions and set a Cowboys franchise record with 1,749 receiving yards, earning first-team All-Pro honors. In August 2024 he signed a four-year, $136 million extension with Dallas. Early in the 2026 season he remained the Cowboys' No. 1 receiver, and on 4 October 2026 he caught 17 passes for 189 yards, including the game-winning touchdown, in a 34–30 win at Houston; through five games he had 39 receptions for 507 yards and four touchdowns.

name: Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History
aliases: The Wright Museum; International Afro-American Museum
description: The Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History in Detroit was founded in 1965 by Dr. Charles H. Wright, an obstetrician, together with thirty other founders, as the International Afro-American Museum; it opened in January 1966 at 1549 West Grand Boulevard. The museum's current home, a 125,000-square-foot facility at 315 East Warren Avenue, opened in 1997. Its collection holds more than 35,000 artifacts, and its core exhibition, And Still We Rise, spans 22,000 square feet. The museum houses the National Museum of the Tuskegee Airmen and produces the annual African World Festival. Its rotunda has served the nation's mourning: Rosa Parks lay in state there in 2005 and Aretha Franklin in 2018. The Wright is one of the largest African American history museums in the United States and the institutional anchor of Detroit's cultural center.

name: Cab Calloway
description: Cab Calloway (Cabell Calloway III, born December 25, 1907, Rochester, New York; died November 18, 1994, Hockessin, Delaware) was the singer, bandleader, and entertainer whose “hi-de-ho” scat made him the swing era's most theatrical frontman. Raised in Baltimore, he briefly attended law school in Chicago — Crane College — while singing in Chicago nightclubs, then reached New York in 1929 and sang “Ain't Misbehavin'” in Fats Waller's revue Connie's Hot Chocolates. From 1931 his orchestra was a house band at Harlem's Cotton Club alongside Duke Ellington's. “Minnie the Moocher,” first recorded in 1931, became the first record by a Black musician to sell one million copies, and his band employed Dizzy Gillespie, Ben Webster, Cozy Cole, and Milt Hinton. Calloway appeared in Stormy Weather (1943) and, at seventy-two, in The Blues Brothers (1980). He received the National Medal of Arts in 1993; “Minnie the Moocher” entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999 and the National Recording Registry in 2019.

name: Cam Newton
description: Cam Newton, born Cameron Jerrell Newton on 11 May 1989 in Atlanta, Georgia, is a retired American professional football quarterback and media host. After beginning at Florida and a junior-college season at Blinn, he won the Heisman Trophy and the BCS national championship at Auburn in 2010, then was drafted first overall by the Carolina Panthers in 2011. He won NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year, setting rookie quarterback records, and in 2015 became the first African American quarterback to win outright the NFL Most Valuable Player award, leading Carolina to a 15–1 record and Super Bowl 50. Injuries diminished his later Carolina seasons; he played for New England in 2020 and returned to Carolina for his final season in 2021, finishing second all-time in quarterback rushing touchdowns. In media, he built his own platforms — the 4th & 1 podcast and Funky Friday — and worked as a First Take analyst for ESPN from 2024 until a July 2026 layoff, after which he continued 4th & 1 as an independent host into October 2026.

name: Claressa Shields
aliases: Claressa Maria Shields; T-Rex; The GWOAT
description: Claressa Shields (born Claressa Maria Shields on 17 March 1995 in Flint, Michigan) is an American professional boxer, self-styled 'GWOAT,' whose career has redrawn what dominance means in women's boxing. Introduced to the sport by her father, she won the middleweight gold medal at the 2012 London Olympics — the first Olympic women's boxing tournament — at seventeen, and repeated the feat at Rio in 2016, becoming the first American boxer to win consecutive Olympic golds. She turned professional in November 2016 and collected world titles across five weight classes, holding all four major belts simultaneously in three divisions, a feat no other boxer, male or female, had achieved in the four-belt era. On 2 February 2025, in her hometown of Flint, she outpointed Danielle Perkins to become the first undisputed women's heavyweight champion in history. She defended that crown against Lani Daniels in July 2025 and, on 22 February 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, won every round on all three cards in a rematch with Franchón Crews-Dezurn, remaining undefeated.

name: Colored World Series
description: The Colored World Series was the championship series of Black baseball, played in two eras. From 1924 through 1927 it matched the champion of the Negro National League against the champion of the Eastern Colored League, taking the name Colored World Series; the Kansas City Monarchs won the first edition in 1924, defeating Hilldale in a best-of-nine series, Hilldale won the 1925 rematch, and the Chicago American Giants took the 1926 and 1927 series over the Bacharach Giants. After a long gap in which no interleague series was held, the championship resumed from 1942 through 1948 between the second Negro National League and the Negro American League, by then generally called the Negro World Series. The Monarchs again won the first series of the new era, sweeping the Homestead Grays in 1942; the Grays won three titles, and the Cleveland Buckeyes, Newark Eagles, and New York Cubans won one each before the final series in 1948. The Monarchs were the only club to appear in both eras.

name: Cheryl Dunye
description: Cheryl Dunye (born May 13, 1966, Monrovia, Liberia) is a Liberian American filmmaker, director, and actor raised in Philadelphia and based in Oakland, California. She earned a B.A. in Film and Media Arts at Temple University in 1990 and an M.A. at Rutgers University's Mason Gross School of the Arts, and first made short experimental works that blended documentary and fiction, a form she called the 'dunyementary.' Her debut feature, The Watermelon Woman (1996), in which she plays a Black lesbian filmmaker researching an erased 1930s actress, made her the first out Black lesbian to direct a narrative feature film. The film won the Teddy Award at the Berlin International Film Festival and entered the National Film Registry in 2021. Dunye has since directed independent features including the HBO film Stranger Inside and many television episodes, and co-founded the Oakland production company Jingletown Films.

name: Cool Papa Bell
aliases: James Thomas Bell; James Thomas Nichols (birth name)
description: James “Cool Papa” Bell (1903–1991) was the fastest star of the Negro leagues and one of the finest center fielders in baseball history. Born James Thomas Nichols outside Starkville, Mississippi, he moved to St. Louis in 1920 and signed with the St. Louis Stars in 1922 as a knuckleball pitcher; manager Bill Gatewood moved him to the outfield, turned him toward switch-hitting, and — legend holds — gave him his nickname after he calmly struck out Oscar Charleston. Bell anchored three of Black baseball's greatest teams: the St. Louis Stars of 1928–1931, the Pittsburgh Crawfords of 1932–1936, and the Homestead Grays of 1943–1945, playing in eight East-West All-Star Games. Contemporaries rated him the fastest man on the basepaths; Paige's tall tales built his legend, but the documented record — a .300-plus bat across two decades, topping .400 on occasion — needs no embroidery. Barred from the majors by segregation, Bell finished playing in the mid-1940s, later scouted and coached, and worked as a St. Louis city hall custodian and night watchman. He was elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1974 and died in St. Louis in 1991.

name: Chris Eubank
aliases: Christopher Livingstone Eubank; Chris Eubank Sr.; Simply the Best
description: Christopher Livingstone Eubank, born 8 August 1966 in Dulwich, London, is a British former professional boxer, usually styled Chris Eubank Sr. since his son Chris Eubank Jr. became a leading fighter. Raised partly in Jamaica and in Peckham, and sent at sixteen to live in New York, where he took up boxing, Eubank turned professional in 1985 in Atlantic City. He won the WBO middleweight title by stopping Nigel Benn in November 1990, beginning one of British boxing's fiercest rivalries, and then held the WBO super-middleweight title from 1991 to 1995, reigning as a world champion for more than five years in total. Famous for his monocle, cane, diction and showmanship as much as for his durability, he finished his career in 1998 with a record of 45 wins, 5 losses and 2 draws. In 2025 he was reconciled publicly with his son at the two Eubank-Benn family fights, appearing at the November rematch.

name: Cyril Ramaphosa
description: Cyril Ramaphosa, born 17 November 1952 in Johannesburg, South Africa, and raised in Soweto, is a South African politician, trade-union leader and businessman who has been president of South Africa since February 2018 and president of the African National Congress (ANC) since 2017. Detained twice under apartheid security laws for his student activism in the 1970s, he completed a law degree in 1981 and in 1982 became the founding general secretary of the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM), building it into one of the country's most powerful unions and helping to found the COSATU federation in 1985. Elected ANC secretary-general in 1991, he served as the ANC's chief negotiator in the multiparty talks that ended apartheid, then chaired the Constitutional Assembly that drafted South Africa's post-apartheid constitution from 1994 to 1996. After a career in business, he returned as ANC deputy president in 2012 and deputy president of the country in 2014. He succeeded Jacob Zuma as president on 15 February 2018, won a full term in 2019, and was reelected in June 2024 at the head of a government of national unity after the ANC lost its outright majority. He remained in office in October 2026.

name: Charlie Sampson
description: Charles Osgood Sampson is an American former professional rodeo cowboy who specialized in bull riding. Born in Los Angeles, California, on July 2, 1957, he found horses as a boy through a stable near Gardena, where wranglers taught him to rope and ride, and he admired African American bull rider Myrtis Dightman. Sampson qualified for the National Finals Rodeo in 1981 and won the Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association world champion bull rider title in 1982, becoming the first African American ever to win that PRCA title. The National Cowboy and Western Heritage Museum notes that his win came eighteen years after Dightman first competed at the National Finals Rodeo. His career lasted almost twenty years, with repeated National Finals Rodeo trips, circuit championships, and severe injuries documented in contemporary reporting. He retired after the National Circuit Finals Rodeo in Pocatello, Idaho, in 1994. He was inducted into the ProRodeo Hall of Fame in 1996, received the Professional Bull Riders Ring of Honor in 2004, and was inducted into the Bull Riding Hall of Fame in 2019. In 2025 an inaugural rodeo bearing his name was staged in Norco, California.

name: Cuban X-Giants
description: The Cuban X-Giants were a professional Black baseball team formed from defecting members of the Cuban Giants, a split dated to 1896 in one account and to a rival side forming in 1895 in another. Like the original Giants, the early X-Giants were not Cuban, although the club later signed Cuban players. Business manager Edward B. Lamar Jr. ran the team, which the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum describes as the dominant Eastern club of the late 1890s and early 1900s. In 1897 the X-Giants beat the Cuban Giants two games to one. Frank Grant joined in 1898, and Sol White was with the club until 1900. In 1903, with Rube Foster pitching, the X-Giants took five of seven games from the Philadelphia Giants for the Eastern title; Philadelphia reversed the result in 1904 after signing Foster away. John Henry Lloyd played his first professional season with the club in 1906. The team became a founding member of the National Association of Colored Baseball Clubs of the United States and Cuba in late 1906 and folded before play began in 1907.

name: Ceaser Emanuel
description: David Emanuel, known as Ceaser Emanuel, born 5 June 1979 in the Bronx, New York, is an American tattoo artist, entrepreneur and reality television personality. Trained in graphic arts, he opened his first Black Ink tattoo studio in Harlem in 2011, building the shop as a Black-owned business in an industry with few Black corporations. VH1's Black Ink Crew, which premiered in 2013, followed Emanuel and the staff of his Harlem shop and made him the face of a franchise that expanded to other cities; he also appeared on VH1's Love & Hip Hop programmes. At his peak he reported owning shops in New York, Atlanta, Orlando and New Orleans. VH1 cut ties with him in June 2022. In an August 2025 interview he said he currently owned four shops, in Brooklyn, Atlanta, Indianapolis and Milwaukee, and was downsizing after suffering two strokes attributed to high blood pressure.

name: Carole Simpson
description: Carole Simpson is a retired American broadcast journalist, news anchor and author from Chicago. A graduate of the University of Michigan, she began her career on radio at WCFL in Chicago and in 1965 became the first woman and the first African American woman to broadcast radio news in Chicago. She was later hired at WBBM, moved to television at Chicago's WMAQ, and joined NBC News in 1975, becoming the first African American woman to anchor a major network newscast. She joined ABC News in 1982 and anchored the weekend edition of World News Tonight from 1988 until October 2003. In 1992 she became the first woman of color to moderate a presidential debate, moderating the Richmond, Virginia debate among George H. W. Bush, Bill Clinton and Ross Perot, and that year received the Journalist of the Year Award from the National Association of Black Journalists. She established the Carole Simpson Scholarship in 1991 for minority students in electronic journalism. She retired from ABC News in 2006, taught journalism at Emerson College in Boston until 2019, and published her autobiography, Newslady, in 2010.

name: Colored Press Association
aliases: National Colored Press Association; American Press Association (later name)
description: The Colored Press Association was the nineteenth-century trade association of African American newspaper editors and publishers, formed after Black newspapers were barred from membership in the Associated Press. What was thought to be the first National Colored Press Convention was held in Louisville, Kentucky, in August 1880. The first organizational meeting of African American editors and publishers followed in Louisville in 1881, and the next two meetings, held in Washington, D.C., resulted in the formation of the National Colored Press Association. The National Park Service's nomination history for the T. Thomas Fortune House records that Fortune's former employer, John Wesley Cromwell, called a convention of Black editors and publishers in Louisville in order to establish the Colored Press Association, a step that benefited Fortune's rise as a racial spokesman. The organization's name was eventually changed to the American Press Association, whose first president was John 'J.Q.' Adams of Louisville. The association operated as the Black press's trade association until it became defunct, and in 1909 the National Negro Press Association was organized in its place, with its first convention also held in Louisville.

name: Celeste Headlee
description: Celeste Headlee is an American journalist, public-radio host, speaker, and author whose career has centered on the craft of conversation. Her official biography records a long public-radio career in which she served as executive producer of On Second Thought at Georgia Public Broadcasting and anchored or hosted programs including Tell Me More, Talk of the Nation, Here and Now, All Things Considered, 1A, and Weekend Edition. She co-hosted the national morning program The Takeaway, from PRI and WNYC, anchored presidential coverage in 2012 for PBS World Channel, and continues as a regular guest host on NPR and American Public Media. Her TEDx talk on having better conversations is counted among the most-watched talks on TED's homepage, though the opened sources give different view totals, shown in this record's statistics rather than blended. She is the author of bestselling books including We Need to Talk, Do Nothing, and Speaking of Race, is president and CEO of the nonprofit Headway DEI, and is the granddaughter of composer William Grant Still. A 2026 publisher biography adds that she teaches journalism at Morgan State University and that a new book, Freedom's Daughters, was scheduled for release in October 2026.

name: Charles Burnett
description: Charles Burnett is an American independent filmmaker, writer, and director born in Mississippi and raised in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences records that he wrote, directed, produced, photographed, and edited his first feature, Killer of Sheep, in 1977 — a portrait of a slaughterhouse worker and his family in Watts that the MacArthur Foundation notes the Library of Congress designated as one of twenty-five significant motion pictures included in the National Film Registry in 1990. Burnett had received a MacArthur Fellowship in 1988. His features include My Brother's Wedding (1983), To Sleep with Anger (1990) — which the MacArthur Foundation describes as the story of three generations of a middle-class African American family in Los Angeles disrupted by a mysterious visitor — The Glass Shield, and Namibia: The Struggle for Liberation, alongside documentaries and television films including Nightjohn, Selma, Lord, Selma, and Nat Turner: A Troublesome Property. He took degrees at Los Angeles City College and at UCLA, earning his M.F.A. in 1973. In 2017 the Academy presented him an Honorary Award Oscar at its Governors Awards, and the Associated Press interviewed him in April 2025, at eighty-one, for the 4K restoration of Killer of Sheep.

name: Carl Rowan
description: Carl Thomas Rowan was an American journalist, author and government official born on August 11, 1925, in Ravenscroft, Tennessee, and raised in McMinnville. He graduated from Bernard High School in 1942 as class president and valedictorian, and in 1944 became one of the first fifteen African Americans commissioned as officers in the United States Navy. After the war he earned a bachelor's degree at Oberlin College in 1947 and a master's degree in journalism from the University of Minnesota in 1948. At the Minneapolis Tribune he became the paper's first Black general assignment reporter in 1950, and his reporting on Southern civil-rights cases won the Sigma Delta Chi award for three consecutive years. President Kennedy appointed him deputy assistant secretary of state and then ambassador to Finland. President Johnson named him director of the United States Information Agency in 1964, making him the highest-ranking Black American in the government at that time. From 1965 he wrote a nationally syndicated column, distributed to sixty newspapers, alongside radio commentary and books including his 1991 autobiography. He retired from syndication in 1999.

name: Charles R. Drew
aliases: Charles Richard Drew; Dr. Charles Drew
description: Charles Richard Drew was an American surgeon and medical researcher born June 3, 1904, in Washington, DC, and a gifted college athlete at Amherst. He earned his medical degrees at McGill University in 1933, graduating second in a class of 137, then joined Howard University College of Medicine and Freedmen's Hospital in Washington. At Columbia University his doctoral research on blood preservation, presented in his dissertation on banked blood, made him the first African American to earn a doctor of medical science degree from Columbia. That work led him to direct the Blood for Britain project, which collected 14,556 donations and shipped over 5,000 liters of plasma to England, and then to help build the American Red Cross blood program, including mobile donation units known as bloodmobiles. He publicly criticized the segregation of donated blood as unscientific. In October 1941 he returned to Howard as head of surgery and chief surgeon at Freedmen's Hospital, devoting the rest of his career to training Black surgeons. He died April 1, 1950, in North Carolina after an automobile accident.

name: Clarence Thomas
description: Clarence Thomas is an American jurist who has served as an associate justice of the United States Supreme Court since October 23, 1991. He was born June 23, 1948, in the Pin Point community near Savannah, Georgia, and was raised in a poor family. He received an A.B., cum laude, from Holy Cross College and a J.D. from Yale Law School in 1974. Admitted to practice in Missouri that year, he served as an assistant attorney general of Missouri from 1974 to 1977, as an attorney with the Monsanto Company from 1977 to 1979, and as a legislative assistant to Senator John Danforth from 1979 to 1981. He then served as assistant secretary for civil rights at the U.S. Department of Education in 1981–82 and as chairman of the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission from 1982 to 1990. In 1990 he became a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. President George H. W. Bush nominated him to the Supreme Court to replace Thurgood Marshall; after reopened hearings on allegations by Anita Hill, the Senate confirmed him 52 to 48.

name: Claude McKay
description: Claude McKay was a Jamaican-born American poet and novelist and a leading voice of the Harlem Renaissance. Born September 15, 1889, in Jamaica — the Poetry Foundation gives Sunny Ville and Britannica gives Nairne Castle — he was the son of peasant farmers, tutored by his brother and by Walter Jekyll, who urged him to write in Jamaican dialect. His first books, Songs of Jamaica and Constab Ballads, appeared in 1912, and he used an award for the former to travel to the United States that year. After brief study at Tuskegee Institute and Kansas State, he settled in New York in 1914 and published in The Liberator, including the protest poetry that made his reputation. Spring in New Hampshire (1920) and Harlem Shadows (1922) established him as a militant voice against racism. After years in the Soviet Union, France, Spain and Morocco, he published Home to Harlem in 1928, described by Britannica as the most popular novel by a Black American author to that time, followed by Banjo and Banana Bottom. He became a U.S. citizen in 1940 and died in Chicago.

name: Charles Burroughs
description: Charles Gordon Burroughs was a Chicago poet who, with his wife, Margaret Taylor-Burroughs, co-founded the museum now known as the DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center. The two married on December 23, 1949. In their home at 3806 South Michigan Avenue in Chicago's Bronzeville neighborhood, on the South Side, they started the Ebony Museum of Negro History and Art, chartered on February 16, 1961. The couple cleared the first-floor parlor of the house for the museum and filled rooms with art and objects they had collected from Africa and pieces friends had offered. The museum, created to preserve, study, and teach Black history and art, ran classes on how to teach Black history and drew visiting students. It was renamed for Jean Baptiste Point du Sable in 1968 and moved in 1973 to a former park administration building in Washington Park. Britannica describes the institution as the oldest independently owned museum in the United States dedicated to African American history and culture, holding more than 15,000 pieces of art and historical memorabilia, and a Smithsonian Institution affiliate. Charles Burroughs died in 1994, after forty-five years of marriage.

name: Charlton D. McIlwain
description: Charlton Deron McIlwain, born in 1971, is an American scholar of race, media, and technology. He earned a B.A. in family psychology from Oklahoma Baptist University in 1994 and a master's degree in human relations and a Ph.D. in communication from the University of Oklahoma, completing the doctorate in 2001. He joined the faculty of New York University in 2001 and is Professor of Media, Culture, and Communication at NYU's Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development, where his work focuses on the intersections of race, digital media, and racial justice activism. He also serves as NYU's Vice Provost for Faculty Engagement and Development and founded the university's Center for Critical Race and Digital Studies. His early books, Death in Black and White (2003) and When Death Goes Pop (2005), studied death, media, and community. With Stephen M. Caliendo he co-authored the award-winning Race Appeal: How Candidates Invoke Race in U.S. Political Campaigns and co-edited The Routledge Companion to Race and Ethnicity (2010). His Black Software: The Internet and Racial Justice, From the AfroNet to Black Lives Matter, published by Oxford University Press, traces Black engagement with computing and the internet from the AfroNet era to Black Lives Matter.

name: Curtis McClain
description: Curtis McClain is a Chicago house-music vocalist best known as the singer on "Move Your Body," the 1986 Marshall Jefferson record subtitled "The House Music Anthem." McClain was Jefferson's friend and a fellow post-office worker, and his vocal on the track was uncredited on its release. The song, among the earliest house records to feature piano, circulated in Chicago clubs on cassette in 1985 before Trax Records released it in June 1986. McClain sang as the vocalist of On The House, the Jefferson-led project that followed the record; the group's own 1986 Trax releases included "Ride The Rhythm," and the Jack Said What label notes that the vocals on "Move Your Body" and the subsequent On The House tracks were all sung by McClain, with Jefferson as the project's main producer. The label also records that the pair were not paid by Trax Records for that work. McClain and Jefferson later revived On The House together, releasing the single "City Life," credited to Curtis McClain and Marshall Jefferson present On The House, on the Jack Said What label on March 22, 2023, with McClain singing over Jefferson's piano chords and strings.

name: California Eagle
aliases: The California Eagle; The Owl; Eagle
description: The California Eagle was a weekly Los Angeles newspaper serving African American readers, published from 1879 to 1964. John J. Neimore founded it in 1879 as The Owl and later renamed it the Eagle. Charlotta Bass, who had arrived in Los Angeles in 1910 and sold subscriptions for the paper, bought it after Neimore's death in 1912, became its editor, and renamed it the California Eagle; her husband, Joseph Blackburn Bass, served as editor until his death in 1934. Under the Basses the paper campaigned against segregation in employment, housing, and transportation, and during the Great Migration it carried practical information on jobs and housing for newly arrived readers. Its circulation reached 60,000 in the 1920s, by 1925 the largest of any African American newspaper in California. Bass owned and operated the paper until 1951, when she sold it to Loren Miller, the paper's former city editor and a civil liberties lawyer. Miller sold the paper in 1963 after his appointment as a Superior Court judge, and the California Eagle ceased publication on January 7, 1964, after eighty-five years. Its offices stood at 4071-4075 South Central Avenue in Los Angeles.

name: Charlotta Bass
aliases: Charlotta Amanda Spears Bass; Charlotta Spears Bass
description: Charlotta Amanda Spears Bass was a Los Angeles newspaper editor-publisher and civil rights activist. Born in Sumter, South Carolina — sources vary on her birth year, placing it between 1874 and 1888 — she sold subscriptions for a Black newspaper in Rhode Island before moving to Los Angeles in 1910 for her health. There she joined The Eagle, the oldest Black newspaper on the West Coast. When its founder John Neimore died in 1912, she bought the paper at auction with fifty borrowed dollars, renamed it The California Eagle, and, with her husband Joseph Bass as editor, built it from a four-page tabloid into a twenty-page weekly that by the 1930s was the largest Black newspaper on the West Coast, with a circulation of about 60,000. From its pages she campaigned against employment discrimination, restrictive housing covenants, police violence, and the Ku Klux Klan. She sold the Eagle in 1951. In 1952 she ran for Vice President of the United States on the Progressive Party ticket with Vincent Hallinan, becoming the first Black woman nominated for that office; the ticket won more than 140,000 votes nationwide. She died in Los Angeles in 1969.

name: Chester Himes
aliases: Chester Bomar Himes; Chester B. Himes
description: Chester Bomar Himes (July 29, 1909 – November 12, 1984) was an American writer born in Jefferson City, Missouri. He attended Ohio State University, then was jailed at the Ohio State Penitentiary from 1929 to 1936 for armed robbery, and began writing fiction in prison, publishing stories in Esquire and other American magazines. After his release he worked at numerous odd jobs and joined the Works Progress Administration, eventually serving as a writer with the Ohio Writers' Project. His first novel, If He Hollers Let Him Go (1945), details the fear, anger, and humiliation of a Black employee of a racist defense plant during World War II. Lonely Crusade (1947) concerns racism in the labour movement, Cast the First Stone (1952) portrays prison life, and The Third Generation (1954) examines family life. In the mid-1950s Himes moved to Paris, where he wrote chiefly murder mysteries set in Harlem, featuring detectives Grave Digger Jones and Coffin Ed Johnson, including The Crazy Kill (1959), Cotton Comes to Harlem (1965), and Blind Man with a Pistol (1969). He won France's Grand Prix de Littérature Policière in 1958, later moved to Moraira, Spain, and died there in 1984.

name: Chicken Bone Beach
description: Chicken Bone Beach, formally Missouri Avenue Beach, is the section of Atlantic City, New Jersey's ocean beach between Missouri and Mississippi Avenues, at the foot of Missouri Avenue near the city's Northside neighborhood. Before 1900, Black and white residents used Atlantic City's beaches together; around 1900, hotel owners pushed Black beachgoers down to the Missouri Avenue beach, south of the Million Dollar Pier, to appease guests from the Jim Crow South, and it remained the city's Blacks-only beach until the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Its nickname came from the fried-chicken picnic lunches families brought because many eating establishments would not serve them. By the 1940s Black entrepreneurs provided summer-evening entertainment, and performers who played the city's Black venues, among them Sammy Davis Jr., Louis Jordan, the Mills Brothers, and Jackie “Moms” Mabley, drew visitors; Club Harlem showgirls called the beach Sunshine Row. Martin Luther King Jr. was photographed on a family vacation there in 1956. In 1997 the Atlantic City Council passed an ordinance declaring Chicken Bone Beach a historical landmark, and the Chicken Bone Beach Historical Foundation installed a commemorative marker in 2015.

name: Clara Ward
description: Clara Mae Ward (April 21, 1924 – January 16, 1973) was a gospel singer, songwriter, and arranger born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Her mother, Gertrude Ward, founded the family group that became the Ward Singers in 1931; Clara recorded her first solo song in 1940, and after a breakthrough appearance at the National Baptist Convention in Philadelphia in 1943 the group began touring nationally. As leader of the Famous Ward Singers, Ward adopted the lead-switching style previously used by male gospel quartets, creating opportunities for soloists such as Marion Williams to take the lead on songs including “Surely God Is Able,” “How I Got Over,” and “Packin' Up.” “Surely God Is Able” was among the first million-selling gospel hits, and the group's album of that name was the first by a gospel group to exceed sales of 500,000 units. From 1943 to 1957 the Ward Singers traveled more than a million miles on the gospel circuit. In the 1960s Ward took the group into nightclubs and other secular venues, a move gospel traditionalists contested, and one that strained her longtime friendship with Mahalia Jackson. She died in Los Angeles, California, on January 16, 1973, after a series of strokes.

name: Cosmopolitan Chamber of Commerce
description: The Cosmopolitan Chamber of Commerce is a Chicago business trade association founded in 1933 to address the concerns of African American business owners. The Chamber describes itself as a nonprofit 501(c)(3) organization and one of the nation's oldest multicultural trade associations. Its membership, as Black Enterprise described it in 1994, comprises major corporations, small and minority-owned businesses, minority- and majority-controlled banks, cultural and educational institutions, and aspiring entrepreneurs. The Chamber provides business and entrepreneurial training classes, computer-application instruction, business counseling, and technical assistance, and it serves minority- and female-owned businesses, seniors, and students through long-standing alliances with neighborhood chambers of commerce, industry associations, governmental agencies, major public and private enterprises, and academic institutions. In 1994 the Chamber facilitated the Tanqueray Emerging Entrepreneurs Program, run in association with Black Enterprise, which supplied four Chicago-area African American entrepreneurs with established mentors and the equivalent of $10,000 each in cash, equipment, and services. A business directory listing records the Chamber as established in 1933 and incorporated in Illinois, listing an address at 30 East Adams Street in Chicago.

name: Columbia Records
aliases: Columbia Phonograph Company; Columbia Recording Corporation; CBS Records
description: Columbia Records is an American record label, headquartered in New York City and owned today by Sony Music Entertainment. It was founded on January 15, 1889, as the Columbia Phonograph Company in Washington, D.C., taking its name from the District of Columbia, and it is described as the oldest surviving brand name in the recorded-sound business and one of Sony Music's flagship labels. On December 17, 1938, the American Record Corporation, including the U.S. Columbia label, was acquired by the Columbia Broadcasting System. Under CBS the label recorded, among many others, Bessie Smith in an earlier Columbia era, and later Miles Davis and Herbie Hancock. Davis's Kind of Blue was released by Columbia on August 17, 1959, and Hancock's Head Hunters was released on Columbia on October 26, 1973. In 1988 Sony acquired the CBS Records Group, including Columbia; the parent division was renamed Sony Music Entertainment in 1991. Columbia remains in label and institution scope — a recording company and brand, not a genre or a catalog — consistent with the graph's Motown and Chess records.

name: Cash Money Records
description: Cash Money Records is a New Orleans record label founded in 1991 by brothers Ronald "Slim" Williams and Bryan "Birdman" Williams (also credited as Bryan "Baby" Williams). Built first on local New Orleans releases, the label signed B.G., Lil Wayne and Juvenile in its early-to-mid-1990s wave, and in May 1997 Birdman organized the Hot Boys, the Cash Money group that helped attract Universal Records. In March 1998 Cash Money became a Universal imprint under a pressing and distribution arrangement whose reported value is contested in the sources and is not asserted here. Wayne, the label's flagship artist for two decades, launched Young Money Entertainment in 2005 as a Cash Money imprint and joint venture. Cash Money's commercial peak is documented in releases including Lil Wayne's Tha Carter III, released by Cash Money on June 10, 2008, and in later signings including Drake and Nicki Minaj. The label is listed as active, distributed in the United States by Republic Records, and was publicly billed as a participating label in an October 2025 Verzuz event.

name: Chicago International Film Festival
description: The Chicago International Film Festival is Chicago's annual international film festival, founded in 1964 by filmmaker and graphic designer Michael Kutza — who was 22 and worked with silent-screen star Colleen Moore — and presented by Cinema/Chicago, the year-round nonprofit cultural and educational organization Kutza also founded. The festival made its debut on November 9, 1965, at the Carnegie Theatre at Rush and Oak Streets, and Cinema/Chicago bills it as North America's longest-running competitive international film festival. Its juried prizes are the Hugo Awards, headed by the Gold Hugo for Best Film in the International Feature Film Competition, with Silver Hugos and category Gold Hugos across the New Directors, International Documentary and OutLook (Q-Hugo) competitions. Kutza served as artistic director through 2017 — longer, the organization notes, than any other festival artistic director — before passing the role to Mimi Plauché. The 62nd edition ran October 14–25, 2026, across the AMC NEWCITY 14, the Music Box Theatre, the Gene Siskel Film Center, the Chicago History Museum and the Reva and David Logan Center for the Arts, where 11 films and An Evening with Marlon Wayans played on the South Side, October 16–22. The edition presented 113 feature films and 57 shorts from 60 countries and marked the 30th anniversary of the festival's Black Perspectives program (CTL-E-6301).

name: Cinema/Chicago
description: Cinema/Chicago is the Chicago nonprofit cultural and educational organization that presents the Chicago International Film Festival. Founded in 1964 — its founder, Michael Kutza, served as its chief executive until his retirement at the end of 2018 and remains CEO Emeritus — the organization states its mission as fostering better communication between people of diverse cultures through the art of film and the moving image, and serving Chicago's diverse and under-served audiences with access to world-class cinema. Beyond the October festival, Cinema/Chicago runs year-round programs: the CineYouth Festival each April, showcasing filmmakers 22 and under; the free Summer Screenings series; Community Cinema, bringing free screenings to under-resourced neighborhoods across the city; the Digging Deeper into Movies lecture series with Northwestern University professor Nick Davis; the Chicago Industry Exchange Lab (CIX:Lab), a creative-development program for emerging Illinois filmmakers; and the Black Perspectives program, the festival's year-round showcase for Black American and African-diaspora cinema since 1997. In 2026 the organization was named a Make It Better Foundation Philanthropy Award recipient, and the festival it presents was voted the No. 2 Best Film Festival in the U.S. for 2026 by USA Today readers.

name: Chardai Johnson
description: Chardai Johnson is Managing Director and Head of the Economic Equity Advisory Group at BMO Bank N.A., the bank practice that cultivates relationships with Black-owned businesses to expand access to capital; HOPE Chicago's leadership page confirms the title verbatim. At BMO since 2012, she previously led a U.S. Commercial Banking team serving family-owned and private businesses, was named a Rising Star Women Leader of Banking for 2024, and has held trustee and board roles with the ChiArts Foundation and Horizons for Youth. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Cleopatra Draper
description: Cleopatra Draper is a radio personality at WVON 1690 AM, Chicago's Black talk station, where she has worked in various capacities since 2019 and in January 2025 took the weekday midday slot (9 a.m.–12 noon), succeeding retired host Perri Small. She holds a master's in social work from the University of Illinois Chicago and founded Roses in Roseland, a nonprofit distributing household goods and groceries. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Corey Williams
description: Corey Williams — the Chicago West Side designer Corey Demon Williams — is the designer, stylist, children's author and actor behind GRÉVYI, a Chicago fashion brand presenting streetwear-meets-couture runway collections, including the sold-out Chicago Fashion Week show 'If You Haven't Been to Paris' on the West Side in October 2025; a public biography styles him CEO and Creative Director of GRÉVYI Clothing. He is not the former NBA player of the same name. He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Corinth Jackson
description: Corinth Jackson is Chief of Staff for Obama Presidential Center Operations at the Obama Foundation, where — in her own statement as a Bisnow Chicago Women Leading Real Estate honoree — she leads strategic and operational planning for the Obama Presidential Center, the museum and civic campus in Jackson Park on Chicago's South Side planned to open in June 2026. World Business Chicago listed her in an earlier Center role, Senior Operations Associate, in 2024. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Ciera Bates-Chamberlain
description: The Rev. Ciera Bates-Chamberlain is the founder and Executive Director of Live Free Illinois, which mobilizes Black churches and faith communities across Illinois to end gun violence and mass incarceration and to build safe, economically viable, self-sustained Black communities. The Obama Foundation named her a 2024–2025 USA Leader, crediting her with convening statewide clergy and nonprofit coalitions and developing violence-reduction and gun-violence and incarceration-reform programs. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.
